header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022 | period: 2022-06
text:
Issued: 13 June 2022

JRC MARS Bulletin – Global outlook

Ukraine, June 2022
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022

section: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook Crop monitoring European neighbourhood Ukraine June 2022 Reduced yield outlook for winter crops
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022 | period: 2022-06 | section: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook Crop monitoring European neighbourhood Ukraine June 2022 Reduced yield outlook for winter crops
text:
Adverse weather conditions since the start of the 2021 – 2022 season have led to a poor yield outlook for winter crops in a major part of central and western Ukraine. Fair yields are expected in the east of the country.

After a difficult autumn, winter crops were further affected by colder-than-usual temperatures during spring, which, in central and western Ukraine, were combined with a persistent rainfall deficit. Our regional forecasts show a below-average yield outlook for winter crops in central and western oblasts, whereas fair yields are expected in the eastern half of the country. At country level, our yield forecast is below the historical trend and well below last year’s record level. Currently above-average temperatures are expected, and - depending on their magnitude – these could further reduce the yield potential. In terms of production, this translates to a forecast of

section: 26.88 Mt of wheat, 6.66 Mt of barley, and 3.75Mt of
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022 | period: 2022-06 | section: 26.88 Mt of wheat, 6.66 Mt of barley, and 3.75Mt of
text: rapeseed. About 22% of the forecast soft wheat production, 19% of the forecast winter barley, and 13% of the forecast rapeseed production is in areas that are currently subject to hostilities due to Russia’s war on Ukraine. Hostilities have also led to a sharp decrease in the area sown to spring and summer crops, which will lead to a lower production of spring barley, grain maize, sunflowers and soybeans.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022 | period: 2022-06 | section: Meteorological overview
text: To date the winter crop season has been characterised by significant temperature fluctuations. A colder-than-usual autumn was followed by a warmer-than-usual winter, and by a predominantly colder-than-usual spring. Rainfall has been below average, with the most distinct anomalies in the south-western parts of the country. Above-average rainfall was registered only in December and April.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022 | period: 2022-06 | section: Autumn (Sept – Oct – Nov)
text:
- Drier-than-usual conditions prevailed overall, with rainfall from 30% to 50% below the 1991-2021 longterm average (LTA). October was particularly dry.

- The rain deficit was most pronounced in the southwest, especially in the oblasts of Odesa, Vinnytsya and Khmelnytskiy.

- Temperatures were on average up to 2 °C below the LTA in most of the country, except in the north-western part where slightly above-average temperatures prevailed.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022 | period: 2022-06 | section: Winter (Dec – Jan – Feb)
text:
- Precipitation was abundant and frequent in December, exceeding double the LTA in south-western regions.

- In January, drier-than-usual conditions prevailed in the south (particularly in the oblasts of Odesa and Mykolaiv), while wetter-than-usual conditions continued in the northern half of the country.

- February was drier than usual in most of the winter crops growing areas. A pronounced rain deficit continued to develop in the southern oblasts.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022 | period: 2022-06 | section: Spring (Mar – Apr – May)
text:
- Most of the winter crops growing regions experienced 10% to 30% below-average precipitation during spring.

- Rainfall was particularly scarce in March and May, but abundant in April.

- Significantly warmer-than-usual temperatures prevailed throughout the winter, particularly in January and February. An average positive thermal anomaly (compared with the LTA) of up to 4 °C was recorded in central and eastern Ukraine. In the western oblasts, temperatures were up to 2 °C above the LTA, on average.

- The strongest dry anomalies (mostly up to 50% below the LTA) occurred in the south-western oblasts.

- Colder-than-usual temperatures prevailed throughout spring in a large part of Ukraine, without reaching critically low levels for winter crops.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022 | period: 2022-06 | section: 1 – 15 June
text:
- Dry conditions continued in most of the country during the first week of June. Abundant rainfall is expected during the second week in the westernmost oblasts.

- Warmer-than-usual temperatures (mostly up to 2 °C above the LTA) were recorded in the first week of June and are expected to continue in the coming week, with the strongest anomalies in the south-eastern oblasts. The daily maxima may exceed 30 °C for several days in southern regions.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022 | period: 2022-06 | section: Crop canopy conditions
text:
The map displays the differences between the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) cumulated from 1 to 31 May 2022 and the medium-term average (MTA, 2012-2021) for the same period, in arable land areas. Positive anomalies (in green) reflect above-average canopy density or early crop development while negative anomalies (in red) reflect below-average biomass accumulation or late crop development.

The map above reflects predominately winter crop conditions, as the summer crop season has just started and contributes little to NDVI values. Average to slightly above-average NDVI values predominate in the eastern half of the country, whereas negative anomalies prevail in the western oblasts. The prevalence of positive NDVI anomalies in southern and eastern oblasts is attributed to above-average biomass accumulation in these regions, which was favoured by adequate precipitation in April and in the second half of May. Conversely, biomass accumulation in the western oblasts continued to lag behind, despite the arrival of some rainfall in late May that brought relief to crops after a persistent rain deficit. Compared with the previous season (see June 2021 issue of this Bulletin), the absence of darker green colours and the higher prevalence of negative anomalies in the current map, are partly attributed to delayed crop development due to the colder-than-usual spring.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022 | period: 2022-06 | section: Crop growth conditions Winter crops
text: Mixed conditions have prevailed since the beginning of the season and translated into a suboptimal development of winter cereals, particularly in central and western regions. Yield potentials were consequently reduced, and the yield forecasts at country level are below the historical trend.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022 | period: 2022-06 | section: Crop growth conditions Winter crops
text:
The 2021 sowing campaign progressed well, particularly in October, thanks to the drier-than-usual conditions in most of the country. The Ukrainian Ministry of Agriculture reported a decrease in the sown area of winter soft wheat and winter barley while the area sown to winter rapeseed increased considerably1. The persistently colder-than-usual autumn conditions in the main winter crops growing regions provided a far from optimal start to the season. Despite the timely sowing, winter crops were overall under-developed prior to entering the winter. Moreover, in several southern and western oblasts (e.g. Odesa, Vinnytsya and Khmelnytskiy), the significantly drier-than-usual conditions resulted in poorly developed stands. Winter was significantly warmer than usual, and winter crops were not exposed to any severe cold spell. The start of spring was particularly cold, however. The daily minimum temperatures dropped locally to -12 °C during the first dekad of March. Winter crops were sufficiently hardened and only local frost damage could have occurred. Scarce precipitation during the first quarter of 2022, particularly in the south-west, led to low soil moisture contents when the winter crops restarted their vegetative growth, which negatively affected their yield potential. The arrival of abundant rainfall in April resulted in a slight improvement in soil water conditions for crops in the southern and eastern oblasts (e.g. Kherson, Dnipropetrovsk) but the dry conditions of May led to a new deterioration of the soil water balance in most of the oblasts. In parallel, the continued colder-than-usual temperatures further hampered crop development. Nevertheless, the absence of thermal stress during the stem elongation and heading stages of winter crops contributed to maintaining the yield potential. Overall, fair yields are forecast in the eastern oblasts, while the yields in the south-western oblasts are expected to be significantly below the historical trend. The current weather forecast shows high temperatures in the eastern oblasts, which, depending on their extent and if combined with below-average rainfall could lead to a further reduction of the yield outlook.

1 https://minagro.gov.ua/news/v-ukrayini-zasiali-1911-tis-ga-yaroyi-pshenici
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022 | period: 2022-06 | section: Spring and summer crops
text:
The sowing campaign of spring and summer crops took place from the end of March to early June. There is a significant drop in the areas sown to sunflowers, spring barley and grain maize, when compared with the previous season. The below-average temperatures since the beginning of spring resulted in a delayed crop growth and development.

The sowings of spring wheat and spring barley were mostly performed in the end of March and the first dekad of April, and were finished around mid-May. Sowing of summer crops incurred some delay due to frequent and abundant rainfall during the last two dekads of April, but the dry conditions in May accelerated progress. All summer crops sowings are expected to be completed during the first dekad of June. The projections from the Ukrainian Ministry of Agriculture show a sharp drop in the area of spring barley and sunflowers compared with the previous season, due to Russia’s war against Ukraine2. The growth of spring and summer crops was slowed by the colder-than-usual temperatures in almost all regions. The rain deficit during the first two dekads of May also hampered early crop development, and may already have affected the yield potential of spring crops. The arrival of rainfall in late May followed by increased temperatures which prevailed since early June, particularly in the eastern oblasts, allowed an acceleration of the crop development and the biomass accumulation. The yield potential could be negatively affected, and rainfall is urgently needed. The yields of spring crops are forecast slightly below the historical trend, while summer crops yields are forecast at the trend level. As it is still very early in the season, these forecasts have a wide margin of uncertainty. Weather conditions in the coming weeks, particularly precipitation and temperature, will be paramount for yield formation.

2 https://minagro.gov.ua/news/v-ukrayini-zasiali-1911-tis-ga-yaroyi-pshenici

section: Appendix Crop area and crop phenology – an analysis using Copernicus Sentinel data
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2022 | period: 2022-06 | section: Appendix Crop area and crop phenology – an analysis using Copernicus Sentinel data
text:
Figure 1. Relative winter crop area change derived from 2022 estimates and compared to 2021 winter crop area, aggregated by village council administrative boundary (with a minimum of 500 ha of winter crop area in 2021).

The European Union’s Copernicus Sentinel satellites have been providing high-resolution imagery since 2015. The sensors on board the Sentinel-1 (S-1) and Sentinel-2 (S- 2) can provide spatial detail at 10 m resolution, which makes it possible to map, in most agricultural areas, individual agricultural parcels and to monitor the crop growth and associated crop practices, both in the microwave (S-1) and the optical visual and infrared (S-2) wavelengths. The regular revisits of Sentinel sensors (5 days for S-2, 6 days for S-11) provide regular sampling over the season, in particular for S-1, which is not hindered by atmospheric conditions such as clouds or rain.

The Sentinels are already widely used in crop monitoring activities. Key developments in this application area are 1) the support of “Big Data Analysis” to ensure quick analysis of large volumes of data over entire territories and seasons; 2) the extensive use of novel machine learning techniques to derive relevant indicators (e.g. crop type, parcel preparations, harvest activities); and 3) the combination of the S-1 microwave signals with those of the multi-spectral S-2. The high-resolution Sentinels are already embedded in the monitoring tasks of the Common Agricultural Policy that are managed by the EU Member States, and for which the JRC has developed an open- 1 One of the sensors, Sentinel 1B, failed at the end of 2021 and the revisit of the remaining Sentinel 1A is 12 days.

The JRC’s combined experience is being used to address the urgent need for detailed information on the impact of Russia’s war against Ukraine on the food security situation. Sentinel coverage of Ukraine has had the same revisit density as in the EU for a number of years. This has enabled the team of the Kyiv Polytechnic Institute (led by Prof. Kussul) with whom the JRC works, to create consistent high-resolution crop maps for the period 2019- 2021, which JRC subsequentlyuse as an essential reference set. Our joint analysis uses a phased approach: we started with identifying the winter crops (winter wheat, winter barley and winter rapeseed) with S-2 imagery from the period 1 November 2021 to end of April 2022. We base our method on empirical NDVI thresholds and apply a synchronisation with respect to Growing Degree Days (Tbase=0°C; accounted from 1 October)3, so that we can compare our estimators with previous years. For the years 2019-2021, we can compare our estimators to the crop area determined in the crop maps, in order to understand whether we underestimate or overestimate at a given cutoff date. We aggregate our results at village council level, the third administrative unit level in Ukraine (with oblast and rajon as the first and second administration levels). The results generated up to 15 April 2022 are shown in Figure 1. In a second step, we can derive the profiles for selected winter crop parcels and compare their trends to parcels in the crop maps of previous years. For this analysis, Leaf

Area Index (LAI) is derived from S-2 data and a distinction is made between winter cereals and rapeseed. We combine the profile analysis with the same agrometeorological information as used in the “classical” bulletin approach, which integrates non-crop specific

MODIS observations. A key advantage of our current highresolution Sentinel-based method is that we can isolate crop specific signals.

LAI profiles for distinct winter wheat and winter rapeseed parcels are aggregated at oblast level. Figure 2 shows some of the major producing oblasts. In the oblasts around the Black Sea, winter wheat has reached the flowering stage (LAI peak) and initiated the senescence phase in early June. It shows that the crop growth trends are in the same order of magnitude as in 2019. Southwestern oblasts (e.g. Odes’ka, Vinnyts’ka) display a delayed LAI profile with lower magnitude than 2019 and

2021. The LAI profiles of rapeseed and the phasing of the phenology are in line with 2021. The distinctive LAI minimum in March is due to rapeseed flowering.

text:
Another trend analysis, this one based on NDVI amplitude of detected winter crops, is shown in Figure 3, which points to some significantly lower values, especially in the western and central part of the country. These are the first indicators of an anticipated overall lower yield in these areas compared with 2019.

Figure 3. Map of crop development conditions in Ukraine at village council level, as estimated on 30 May 2022. NDVI amplitude is used as a proxy for crop development. The amplitude of the NDVI temporal profiles was compared against a reference year (2019). The colour palette indicates the relative deviations.

Our next steps include the monitoring of winter crop harvesting and the delineation of the spring and summer crops and performing a similar growth trend analysis to those. For this, we intend to integrate S-1 backscattering coefficients and coherence data as well. S-1 coherence data is particularly useful for detecting changes to the agricultural surface, and the timing of these changes correlate with preparation activities (ploughing, seedbed preparation). Together with more recent S-2 data, this information will thus be useful for determining detected crop areas and cross-check the large deviations in sown area that are reported for major summer crop types like maize and sunflowers. An update on the activities is foreseen for the September special bulletin issue.

title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023

section: Ukraine April 2023 Weather conditions permit fair yield outlook
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023 | period: 2023-04 | section: Ukraine April 2023 Weather conditions permit fair yield outlook
text:
Mild temperatures combined with sufficient rainfall since the start of the 2022-2023 season currently maintain a fair-to-positive yield outlook for winter crops in a major part of Ukraine. However, winter cereal production is forecast significantly below the 5-year average in both government-controlled and non-controlled areas due to reduced sown areas.

A decrease in winter crop sown areas due to the lower availability of labour and agricultural input because of Russia’s war against Ukraine is noted. This does not only apply for the non-government controlled areas, but also in the oblasts under the control of Ukraine. While rapeseed sowing progressed rapidly in August and September 2022, the exceptionally wet conditions during autumn resulted in a slow start to the winter cereal sowing campaign. Nevertheless, the mild temperature allowed favourable germination and early development prior to entering winter. Since then, the unusually warmer-thanusual temperatures throughout the winter and the early spring have allowed winter crops to pass the dormancy period without any detrimental frost damage and to restart their growth under good conditions. More rainfall is needed in the eastern and, especially, southern parts of the country to allow soil moisture conditions to be restored and to avoid future yield losses.

The JRC MARS yield forecasts for winter crops currently follow historical trends. In terms of production, this translates into a forecast of 25.48 Mt of wheat, 3.77 Mt of winter barley and 3.04 Mt of rapeseed, of which 20.67 Mt (wheat), 3.08 Mt (winter barley) and 2.71 Mt (rapeseed) are forecast for the government-controlled areas. These initial forecasts will be revised depending on areas estimate adjustments and on updated MARS yield forecasts during the remaining season.

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023 | period: 2023-04 | section: Meteorological overview
text: To date, in most parts of the country, the winter crop season has been characterised by an exceptionally wet autumn with close-to-average temperatures, followed by an unusually mild winter with close-to-average rainfall. The beginning of spring provided significantly above-average temperatures in most oblasts, with a distinct rain deficit in the southernmost regions.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023

section: Autumn (September, October, November) Exceptionally wet autumn with close-to-average temperatures
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023 | period: 2023-04 | section: Autumn (September, October, November) Exceptionally wet autumn with close-to-average temperatures
text:
- Near-seasonal temperatures and wetter-than-usual conditions prevailed in most of the country during autumn. Temperatures in the southernmost and easternmost oblasts were predominantly slightly above the 1991-2021 long-term average (LTA). Rainfall was particularly abundant in the north-eastern oblasts (e.g. Luhans’ka, Kharkivs’ka), where precipitation reached up to twice the LTA. Odes’ka was the only oblast with below-average rainfall.

- In September, slightly below-average temperatures prevailed. Rainfall was abundant and frequent in most oblasts, most distinctly in the western oblasts (e.g. Lvivs’ka, Rivnens’ka). Below-average rainfall (up to 50% below the LTA) occurred only in parts of the Khersons’ka and Zaporiz’ka oblasts.

- In October, abundant precipitation continued in the northern and eastern oblasts, while a rain deficit was observed in the southern oblasts (e.g. Odes’ka, Vinnyts’ka). Temperatures were up to 2 °C above the LTA in central and eastern parts, and up to 4°C above the LTA in the west.

- In November, abundant precipitation prevailed throughout the country, except in the westernmost oblasts where rainfall was up to 50% below the LTA. Temperatures remained up to 2°C above the LTA in most regions.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023

section: Winter (December, January, February) Unusually mild winter with close-to-average rainfall
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023 | period: 2023-04 | section: Winter (December, January, February) Unusually mild winter with close-to-average rainfall
text:
- Ukraine experienced an exceptionally mild winter, most distinctly in the central and western oblasts where mean daily temperatures exceeded the LTA by up to 4 °C.

- In most parts of the country, winter precipitation was average to slightly below average. A distinct rainfall surplus, with precipitation up to 50% above the LTA, was observed in the westernmost and northernmost oblasts (e.g. Chernihivs’ka, Rivnes’ka). A distinct rainfall deficit was recorded in some southern and eastern oblasts (Odesk’a, Donets’ka), where precipitation was up to 50% below the LTA.

- January was particularly dry and warm for most of the country. In the westernmost oblasts, temperatures were up to 6 °C above the LTA.

- Near-seasonal precipitation prevailed in February, except in the southern and easternmost oblasts where significantly drier-than-usual conditions persisted. Above-average temperatures persisted until the end of the month.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023

section: March Distinct rain deficit in the southernmost regions and mild conditions overall
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023 | period: 2023-04 | section: March Distinct rain deficit in the southernmost regions and mild conditions overall
text:
- Drier-than-usual conditions prevailed throughout most of the country during the first two dekads of March. Precipitation was up to 50% below the LTA in most regions, but more distinct rain deficits (up to 80%) occurred in parts of the southern and western oblasts (e.g. Odes’ka, Vinnyts’ka).

- Substantial rainfall was observed over a large part of the country, while below-average precipitation continued in the south-eastern oblasts during the final days of March.

- Temperatures until 20 March remained -2-4°C above the LTA in most regions, and the mild conditions continued until the end of the month.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023 | period: 2023-04 | section: Crop growth conditions
text:
The rapeseed sowing campaign progressed rapidly, while soft wheat and winter barley sowing was delayed due to wetter-than-usual autumn conditions. However, the predominantly mild temperatures provided favourable conditions for germination and early development. The continued mild temperatures during winter and early spring resulted in the absence of any signicant detrimental frost damage across the country and in the early restart of vegetative growth. Hence, winter crops are in fair-to-good condition and our yield forecasts follow historical trends.

The map displays the differences between the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) cumulated from 1March to 20 March 2023 and the medium-term average (MTA, 2013-2022) for the same period in arable land areas. Positive anomalies (in green) reflect above-average canopy density or early crop development, while negative anomalies (in red) reflect below-average biomass accumulation or late crop development.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023 | period: 2023-04 | section: Crop growth conditions
text: The 2022 rapeseed sowing started in the second dekad of August. Sowing progressed rapidly, with 98% of the sowing completed before 20September, and the final fields completed in the first dekad of October. The oblasts of Dnipropetrovs’ka, Khmelnyts’ka, Vinnyts’ka, Ternopils’ka and Odes’ka are the major rapeseedproducing regions. The sowing campaign for winter wheat and winter barley started slowly during the first dekad of September due to the abundant and frequent rainfall, but progressed well in the last two dekads of October. The mild autumn temperatures allowed sowing to continue until the end of November. According to our estimate, a reduction of 7% compared with the 5-year average in the areas with winter crops is observed in the government-controlled areas. This is likely due to the possible lack of agricultural input and labour to perform the fieldwork. In the non-government-controlled areas, our remotesensing analysis (see appendix) suggests that winter crops were sown and grown during autumn 2022 in the oblasts of Zaporiz’ka, Khersons’ka, Donets’ka and Luhans’ka. Our analysis suggests that the area of winter crops in these regions decreased by 22% compared with the 2021-22 season. Despite the delayed sowing, the wet and mild autumn in the main winter-crop growing regions provided a positive start to the season. Crops were overall sufficiently developed prior to entering winter dormancy, thanks to optimal soil moisture conditions in most regions, except in Odes’ka. The persistent warmer-than-usual conditions throughout the winter prevented winter crops from being exposed to any severe cold spells. Temperatures rarely dropped below −12°C. Hence, our crop model did not signal any detrimental frost damage and shows that winter crops lost most of their frost tolerance quite early compared with the previous season. Our crop model shows that winter crops broke their dormancy period and restarted their vegetative growth from the beginning of spring, while maintaining a fair-topositive yield potential if favourable weather conditions prevail during the rest of spring.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023 | period: 2023-04 | section: Crop growth conditions
text:
Rainfall is needed in the eastern and, especially, southern parts of the country to allow the soil moisture conditions to be restored and to avoid yield losses.

This picture is also confirmed by our remote sensing analysis. In the western parts of the country, the vegetation index indicates an increase in post-winter canopy density compared with the MTA, which is attributed to the favourable weather conditions during autumn and winter. However, in the southernmost part of the country, notably in Odes’ka, south of Mykolayivs’ka, and Crimea, canopy density appears to be below the MTA, most likely due to the persistent rain deficit1. Our yield forecasts for winter crops currently follow historical trends. In the eastern half of the country, we used the 5-year average to attempt to take into account the sub-optimal management practices (machinery, fertilisers, labour, etc.) since the beginning of Russia’s war against Ukraine. In the western half of the country, we assume more stable conditions and, consequently, used a linear trend. Moreover, the dry and warm conditions in March resulted in an early start to the sowing campaign for spring and summer crops. According to the Ukrainian Ministry of Agriculture 2, sowing started early compared with last season and is currently being carried out in all the government-controlled oblasts.

1) The analysis of remote sensing images shows that the majority of the snow cover across the country has melted, but caution must still be taken when interpreting the data since the snow cover for February can be misleading. In the northern and eastern parts, some data errors caused by misclassified snow cover may perturb the signal.

section: Estimation of winter crop area trends using high-resolution remote sensing analysis
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023 | period: 2023-04 | section: Estimation of winter crop area trends using high-resolution remote sensing analysis
text:
We have continued to build on the analysis of highresolution Copernicus Sentinel data, which was initiated in the spring of 20223. This work is coordinated with Kyiv Polytechnic Institute (KPI), which has a unique capacity to generate high-quality synoptic crop maps for the entire Ukrainian territory, and the World Bank team, which implements EU-funded support programmes in land market transparency and, since the start of the Russian war against Ukraine, financial support schemes for the agricultural sector. Our joint work feeds the World Bank econometric impact analysis of the conflict and is highly relevant for assessing the reconstruction needs of the sector4. Furthermore, since Ukraine became a candidate for EU accession in July 2022, elements of this work are increasingly relevant for Ukraine's preparation for the Common Agricultural Policy. Our analysis relies on a progressive and increasingly detailed identification of crops as the growing season advances. Early season winter crop area estimation is based on detecting the NDVI values at parcel level in the period from 1November to the first cut-off date in spring (26March 2023 for this bulletin), as explained below. At this stage in the season, it is not yet possible to distinguish between the major winter crop types (winter wheat, winter barley and rapeseed). Detailed crop maps from previous years are used to limit this analysis to arable land and minimise confusion with permanent grassland. However, the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 has led to land abandonment either directly, due to military actions in the occupied areas, or indirectly, due to other factors that have impacted agricultural production. The severe drought in the spring and summer of 2022, which led to substantial abandonment in the southern oblasts, may have also had a knock-on effect into 2023. The

3) https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC127973 abandonment of arable land is expected to lead to a higher NDVI than that for bare land (due to the regrowth of abandoned crops, weed cover), which could thus contaminate our winter crop cover estimate.

section: Estimation of winter crop area trends using high-resolution remote sensing analysis
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023 | period: 2023-04 | section: Estimation of winter crop area trends using high-resolution remote sensing analysis
text:
The annual crop maps produced by KPI play a key role in our analysis. We can compare our winter crop estimates of previous years to the total area of winter crops in the final crop maps for the same years. Abandonment is likely to be crop-specific, for instance, more likely for unharvested summer crops. The classification accuracy of the annual crop maps is thus essential, and we have developed an independent method to cross-check and confirm the reported high accuracies. For this, we integrate country-wide parcel delineations, which have been produced by the European service company Sinergise

Ltd, with sponsorship from the European Space Agency's

Network of Resources. Sinergise uses an open-source instance segmentation technique to delineate agricultural parcels from Sentinel-2 image stacks for the period 15May to 15 July. The parcel delineations contain around 3.5million features for each year in the series

(2017-2022) representing around 30Mha of arable land.

This excludes most of the grassland and crop cultivation in small parcels, due to masking and filtering, which explains the difference with the total crop area in the KPI crop maps (around 44Mha). The major advantage in using parcel features is the possibility of analysing parcelspecific crop trends with the use of very fast grouped reduction algorithms. This is particularly useful when integrating Sentinel-1 imagery. Since the latter provides consistent and regularly sampled time series that are not affected by cloud cover, they contribute to the robustness of our analysis framework.

text: Figure 1.. Winter crop preparation detection in delineated parcels sorted by 2022 crop type in the Mykolayivs’ka oblast (top) and Donets’ka oblast (bottom). Categories on the x-axis show whether a bare soil state (indicating field preparation) was detected either in September 2022, or in October 2022, or not at all. section: Estimation of winter crop area trends using high-resolution remote sensing analysis
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023 | period: 2023-04 | section: Estimation of winter crop area trends using high-resolution remote sensing analysis
text:
In Figure 1, we illustrate our method to cross-check abandonment. Our hypothesis is that if parcels are abandoned there should be an undisturbed trend towards increasing NDVI, without a clear bare soil transition, since that would indicate preparation for crop cultivation. For parcels sown for winter crops, field preparation should occur in the September-November period and they should then show a NDVI above our threshold (which we set at 0.25) before the cut-off date. We show analysis results for the oblasts of Mykolayivs’ka and Donets’ka, which are on opposite sides of the current conflict frontline. Results are presented for the wheat, maize, sunflower and ‘uncultivated’ crop classes in the 2022 KPI crop map. Most wheat parcels in 2022 show a clear bare soil state in September. Only less than half the area re-emerges as winter crops in 2023, with the remainder left for spring or summer crop preparations. Only a small proportion of parcels show no bare soil state in September or October, about half of which are detected as winter crops. This proportion of parcels may relate to abandonment. For maize, most of the bare soil detection is in October, and only a small proportion is prepared as winter crops. A more significant proportion of maize parcels show no bare soil state, which is likely due to late harvesting. The trends in both oblasts are more or less equal for both wheat and maize. They differ more significantly for sunflower, which shows a higher conversion to winter crops in Mykolayivs’ka than in Donets’ka. This may be related to the more severe drought impact on sunflower in Mykolayivs’ka. An interesting trend is visible in the ‘uncultivated’ crop class of 2022: the majority of parcels exhibit a bare soil state and a significant share emerges as winter crops in 2023.

The small ‘none’ category in this case suggests that permanent abandonment is not particularly evident. The overall conversion to winter crops is significantly higher in

Mykolayivs’ka than in Donets’ka.

section: Estimation of winter crop area trends using high-resolution remote sensing analysis
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, April 2023 | period: 2023-04 | section: Estimation of winter crop area trends using high-resolution remote sensing analysis
text:
Figure 2. Winter crop cover estimate on 26March 2023 vs winter crop occurrence in 2022 (from KPI crop map) aggregated at village council level. Areas with <10% winter crop cover in 2022 are masked.

Figure 2 shows our estimate of trends in winter crop area based on the observations until 26March 2023 compared with their reported occurrence in 2022. Agrometeorological conditions in spring 2023 are comparable to those of 2021, with winter crops that are advanced in development in comparison to the spring of 2022 (see main bulletin). A direct comparison of estimates derived at equivalent growing degree days (GDD) and regressed against the official 2021 figures shows an area decrease in 2023 (8.0 Mha) with respect to both 2021 (9.0 Mha) and 2022 (8.8 Mha). These estimates are for the integral Ukrainian territory, including the occupied areas.

The estimates in the occupied oblasts are 1.8 Mha in 2023 vs 2.3 Mha in 2021, i.e. a drop of 22%. The significant drop in winter crops in the occupied areas needs to be verified with area estimates for spring and summer crops later this season to determine whether it signals a significant increase in abandonment. We stress that the cut-off date of 26 March 2023 currently used is very early in the season and that a more accurate winter crop estimate should preferably include observations until 15 April

2023.

section: June 2023 High levels of winter crops production expected
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: June 2023 High levels of winter crops production expected
text:
Favourable weather conditions continued during spring, and sustained a positive yield outlook for winter crops in most regions. High yields are expected in the southern and eastern parts of the country. Production areas follow the 5-year average despite the Russian war against Ukraine. A record high rapeseed production is expected.

After a mild winter, winter crops restarted their vegetative growth under favourable conditions and the increased temperatures in March boosted their development. The wet conditions of April and the absence of thermal stress in May permitted a positive yield outlook for winter crops. Although field abondonment is observed in several parts of the country, remote sensing analysis suggests that the total acreage of winter crops is higher than in 2022, and is close to the 5-year average in government-controlled and non-controlled areas However, the share of rapeseed has significantly increased in the government-controlled areas, at the expense of soft wheat (see the Appendix for methodological description). The JRC yield forecast for winter crops at country level is currently well above average and close to the record yields of 2021.

In terms of production, this translates into a forecast of
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

section: 28.3 Mt of wheat, 3.7 Mt of winter barley and 5.5 Mt of
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: 28.3 Mt of wheat, 3.7 Mt of winter barley and 5.5 Mt of
text: rapeseed, of which 21 Mt of wheat, 2.9 Mt of winter barley and 5 Mt of rapeseed are in the government-controlled areas. Spring and summer crops sowings were delayed due the wet conditions in April. The area with grain maize has decreased, whereas sunflowers present an increased area. Our yield forecasts for summer crops currently follow the 5-year average.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: Meteorological overview
text: After an exceptionally wet autumn followed by an unusually mild winter, the spring season provided above-average temperatures (particularly in the eastern half of the country), and sufficient rainfall. A distinct rain surplus prevailed in the eastern parts, thanks to record-high precipitation in April. Near-seasonal temperatures are expected during the first half of June, but with drier-than-usual conditions in the north-east.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

section: March Rainfall disparities, but mild temperatures in most oblasts
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: March Rainfall disparities, but mild temperatures in most oblasts
text:
- After drier-than-usual conditions in most oblasts during the first two dekads of March, substantial rainfall arrived during the third dekad.

- Overall, March rainfall was 50% or more above the LTA in the north-western oblasts (e.g. Zhytomyrs’ka, L’vivs’ka), while it was mostly 10% to 30% below the LTA in the rest of the country.

- Temperatures were 2-4°C above the LTA throughout the country. The third dekad was particularly warmer than usual (4-6°C above the LTA) in some central and northernmost oblasts (e.g. Chernihivs’ka, Cherkas’ka).

- The last 2 nights of March were characterised by freezing temperatures, but without dropping below -5°C.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

section: April Record-high rainfall combined with record-low sunshine
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: April Record-high rainfall combined with record-low sunshine
text:
- Frequent and abundant rainfall prevailed during the entire month. Record-high monthly rainfall was registered in most oblasts, reaching more than twice the LTA in several regions (e.g. Zaporiz’ka, Odes’ka, Cherkas’ka).

- During the first two dekads of April, seasonal to slightly colder-than-usual temperatures were recorded in the western half of the country, while a temperature surplus of up to 2°C prevailed in the eastern half.

- During the third dekad, temperatures were up to 2°C below the LTA in most oblasts. Near seasonal temperatures were observed only in the easternmost oblasts.

- Solar radiation was exceptionally low in most parts of the country. The most distinct anomalies (30% or more below the LTA) were recorded in the south (e.g. Mykolayivs’ka).
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

section: May Moderately increasing temperatures, with distinct rain deficit in the western half
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: May Moderately increasing temperatures, with distinct rain deficit in the western half
text:
- During the first two dekads of May, rainfall was rare in most parts of the country (e.g. Kyyivs’ka, Dnipropertovs’ka) and was 30% to 50% below the LTA in the westernmost oblasts (e.g. L’vivs’ka, Volyns’ka).

- Rainfall returned to the eastern half of Ukraine during the third dekad of May, but drier-than-usual conditions continued in the western half.

- May started significantly cooler than usual (2°-4°C below the LTA) but temperatures in the second dekad were near seasonal to slightly above the LTA in most regions.

- During the third dekad, temperatures were mostly up to 2°C above the LTA in the central and western oblasts, while near-seasonal temperatures prevailed in the eastern oblasts.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: 1-15 June
text:
- Significantly drier-than-usual conditions and slightly below-average temperatures prevailed in large parts of the county during the first week of June.

- Abundant rainfall is forecast in the southern and western oblasts during the second week of June, but dry conditions are expected to continue in the with below-average temperature (mostly up to 2°C below the LTA). Temperatures would remain slightly below average levels.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: Crop growth conditions
text:
Winter crops restarted their vegetative growth under favourable conditions and profited from the overall mild spring temperatures to boost their development. The wet conditions in April delayed the sowing progress of spring and summer crops, but considerably improved soil moisture conditions in most regions. The absence of any thermal or hydric stress, sustains a continued positive yield outlook for winter crops. The overall slightly cooler-than-usual temperatures and the return of rainfall expected during the second week of June in the major producing areas provide good conditions for the grain filling of winter cereals.

Due to financial and logistical issues faced by the farmers due to the Russian war against Ukraine, a decrease in the cereals areas against an increase in oilseed crops (rapeseed, sunflowers, soybeans) is reported by the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food1 for the current season. This is also in line with the results of our crop-specific remote sensing analysis for winter crops (see Appendix).

The map displays the differences between the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) cumulated from 1 to 31 May 2023 and the medium-term average (MTA, 2013-2022) for the same period in arable land areas. Positive anomalies (in green) reflect above-average biomass accumulation, while negative anomalies (in red) reflect belowaverage biomass accumulation.

1 https://minagro.gov.ua/news/olijnih-kultur-posiyut-bilshe-virobnictvo-zernovih-zmenshitsya-taras-visockij

The map above reflects predominantly winter crop conditions, as the summer crop season has just started and contributes little to NDVI values. In the western regions of the country, the map indicates a reduced advance in growth of winter crops compared with the previous analysis in March2, which is mainly attributed to the lack of radiation in April, but delayed development of spring and summer crops (due to sowing delays) may also have contributed. Moving to the central parts of the country, the overall situation is positive, with slightly higher than average NDVI values due to the favourable soil moisture and thermal conditions.

In the southern and south-eastern regions, the conditions for crop development have ranged from favourable to very favourable. However, there is a clearly visible reddish band from Khersons’ka to Donets’ka, which corresponds to areas where crop cultivation has been significantly
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: Winter crops
text:
After a delayed start of the season due to the wetterthan-usual conditions during autumn, winter crops entered the winter under favourable conditions for germination and early development. These positive conditions continued throughout the winter, since mild temperatures and close-to-average precipitation prevailed.

The mild temperatures since early March allowed winter cereals to break dormancy and restart their vegetative growth under fair-to-good conditions and earlier than in the spring of 2022. They also resulted in the absence of any detrimental late frost damage across the country.

The abundant and frequent rainfall in April restored soil moisture to adequate levels in most oblasts, and relieved concerns in the areas that had been affected by rainfall deficit at the beginning of the season as reported in the April edition of the Ukraine Bulletin (i.e. southern parts of Odes’ka, Mykolayivs’ka and Khersons’ka). It also permitted winter crops to avoid any hydric stress in the following weeks. However, the exceptionally low levels of sunshine during this period limited photosynthetic activity. In the western oblasts (e.g. L’vivs’ka, Khmel’nyts’ka) where the solar radiation deficit was most pronounced, our crop model indicates deteriorated conditions for winter rapeseed during the flowering phase.

The absence of any significant rainfall in May was predominantly positive, since it prevented the occurrence of water excess during the flowering of winter cereals, and
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: Winter crops
text:
2 https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC133091 reduced due to hazardous conditions near the front line of the Russian war in Ukraine, that prevented farmers from accessing their fields. In the easternmost parts of the country, specifically the non-government controlled areas of Luhans’ka and Donets’ka, the map shows slightly above-average NDVI values, reflecting favourable weather conditions since March. More to the west (e.g. Kharkivs’ka, Poltavs’ka, Sums’ka), the map highlights a significantly below-average NDVI for the given period despite favourable weather conditions since March. This was already observed (to a lesser extent) in the April edition of the Bulletin on Ukraine, and was explained by the possible sub-optimal management practices near the war zone. The delayed sowing of summer crops, especially grain maize, also explains part of the below-average NDVI in these regions.

limited the spread of pest and diseases. Moreover, the overall cooler-than-usual temperatures during this month permitted winter crops to enter the reproductive phase without any thermal stress.

Near-seasonal to cooler-than-usual temperatures and a return of rainfall are expected during the first half of June in the major winter cereals producing regions. This would maintain favourable thermal conditions for the grain formation process.

Based on the above-mentioned predominantly favourable weather conditions and positive remote sensing indicators, our yield forecasts for winter cereals were revised upwards and are now above the historical trends and well above the 5-year average. In the southern and eastern oblasts (e.g. Odes’ka, Khersons’ka, Zaporiz’ka), new record high yields could be achieved if the weather remains favourable in early summer.

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: Winter crops
text: Our forecast for winter rapeseed was also revised upwards in most parts, but remains close to the historical trend in the western oblasts. It is noted that these forecasts do not explicitly account for sub-optimal management due to the logistical and financial issues faced by Ukrainian farmers. For example, a decrease of nitrogen fertilisation or phytosanitary measures may lead to a reduction in the yield potential that we cannot quantify using our yield forecasting system. This could explain the deterioration of the remote sensing indicators in recent weeks. which, however, are still above the 10actually harvested remain subject to a high uncertainty, year average in several oblasts. header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: Summer crops
text: The 2023 spring crops sowing started in the second dekad of March, whereas field operations for summer crops were hampered by the frequent and abundant rainfall of April, and started slowly in the second dekad of April. The first fields of sunflowers were sown around 15 April, while the grain maize and soybean sowings could not start before
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

section: 25 April. Consequently, the sowing campaign was delayed,
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: 25 April. Consequently, the sowing campaign was delayed,
text:
despite a reported acceleration in the second and third dekad of May. Sowings are expected to be completed by mid-June. According to the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food3, an increase of the sunflowers area and a decrease in the grain maize area is reported in the government-controlled areas compared with the 2022 crop season. The warmer-than-usual conditions in the eastern and northern oblasts (e.g. Chernihivs’ka) have allowed normal development of summer crops so far. However, in oblasts without any distinct temperature accumulation surplus (e.g. Cherkas’ka, Vinnyts’ka), the delayed sowing combined with the cooler-than-usual temperature in May resulted in delayed development of spring and summer crops, as indicated by our crop model simulation and remote sensing images. Our yield forecast for spring and summer crops currently follows the 5-year average. However, it is acknowledged that the current delayed crop development, implies a higher-than-usual risk of negative impacts of unfavourable dry and hot conditions during summer. With the destruction of the Nova Kahkvoka dam the irrigation of around 300.000 ha has been jeopardized that were mainly devoted to spring and summer crops.

section: Appendix Crop area and crop phenology – an analysis using Copernicus Sentinel data
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: Appendix Crop area and crop phenology – an analysis using Copernicus Sentinel data
text: Figure 1. Change in green fallow ratio in winter crop cover estimates for 2023 relative to 2021 aggregated at village council (3rd administrative) level. The shift towards the higher ratio levels in 2023 is particularly evident in the conflict zone and the immediate neighboring areas.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: Winter crops detection
text: In the April 2023 edition of the Bulletin4, we described our method to estimate winter crop cover using Copernicus Sentinel data. Our initial estimate used a cut-off date of
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

section: 26 March 2023, which, while providing a reasonable trend,
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: 26 March 2023, which, while providing a reasonable trend,
text: was considered too early for a more reliable area figure. The method was first refined by integrating Growing Degree Day (GDD) normalization at Oblast level [1] before applying the NDVI threshold. This regional refinement provides winter cover estimates at comparable phenological stage rather than the same, fixed date range. Using GDD normalization is especially important in Ukraine, which presents a strong GDD gradient in spring, roughly from South (warmest) to North (coldest). We used the annual crop maps produced by KPI to regress spring and winter crop area estimates against the final official winter crop area estimates for previous years and found GDD = 350 as the most suitable cutoff GDD.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: Abandoned fields (green fallow)
text:
One issue causing uncertainty in the winter crop cover estimate was the effect of abandonment. The analysis described in the April was extended with the use of maximum value composites of Sentinel-1 coherence data [2] for both the periods 1 September to 1 December 2022 and 15 April to 31 May 2023. High values of coherence on arable land are linked to the detection of fallow soil status. True winter crops should appear in our GDD normalized winter crop delineation and should show a bare soil phase

4 https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC133091 in autumn but not in spring. Applying this logic to the 3 data layers is straightforward and can be done retroactively to the 2021 and 2022 data for cross-comparison. A green fallow effect (no bare soil phase in autumn nor in spring) is distinct in 2023. At national level, approximately 7% of winter crop cover was green fallow in 2021 (8% in 2022), whereas it rises to 11.5% in 2023, which corresponds to an increase of almost 600 kha. However, the spatial pattern is more explicit, with Oblasts in and near the military conflict zone showing a significant increase in green fallow (e.g., Kharkivs’ka, from 5 to 20% of winter crop cover) while others show little change (e.g., Rivnens’ka). Nevertheless, regional patterns at village council level (Figure 1) suggest abandoned cultivation also in the government-controlled areas.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: Rapeseed detection
text: The winter crop estimates are used to distinguish rapeseed from winter cereals by determining the so-called “yellow index” [3], using a threshold during the expected flowering period of rapeseed. Flowering is expected in the GDD range 400-450 (counting from 1 January, with Tbase=0°C), which corresponds to late April in Southern oblasts and mid-May in Northern oblasts. The length of the flowering period depends on temperature and solar radiation. Cloud-free Sentinel-2 data for the relevant periods are used to isolate rapeseed.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: Winter Cereal Split
text: The residual winter crop estimate, after deduction of the green fallow and rapeseed classes, is expected to represent the winter cereals, predominantly winter soft wheat and winter barley. These two crop types are not easily separable before the ripening stage (later in June). Therefore, we use the 5-year average share at oblast level to estimate the winter soft wheat and winter barley specific areas.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2023 | period: 2023-06 | section: LAI crop-specific analysis
text:
We extracted the leaf area index (LAI) profiles for winter cereals and rapeseed parcels that were detected following the previously introduced method. We compared their patterns to the parcels depicted in previous years' crop maps. This method, which utilizes high-resolution Sentinel data, provides a significant advantage compared with the method normally used in the Bulletin, based on non-crop specific MODIS observations. At the oblast level, we aggregated the LAI profiles for distinct winter cereals and winter rapeseed parcels. Figure 2 displays some of the main oblasts where these crops are extensively cultivated. In most regions, the onset of spring green-up occurred earlier than in previous years. In some of the eastern oblasts, the LAI reached a five-year high, surpassing the level of 2021 (e.g., Zaporiz’ka). In the Black Sea region, the LAI levels are also in the high range, albeit slightly lower than in 2021 (e.g. Odes’ka). This qualitative analysis of the Sentinel-2 LAI time series overall confirms the excellent growth conditions for winter crops.

Figure 2. Leaf area index (LAI) profiles for winter cereals and winter rapeseed in selected major producing oblasts. Time series are extracted for parcels identified for both crop types and compared to previous years.

JRC MARS Bulletin – Global outlook

Ukraine, September 2023
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023

section: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook Crop monitoring European neighbourhood Ukraine September 2023 Good yield outlook for summer crops, but reduced production of grain maize
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023 | period: 2023-09 | section: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook Crop monitoring European neighbourhood Ukraine September 2023 Good yield outlook for summer crops, but reduced production of grain maize
text:
Throughout the summer of 2023, Ukraine experienced predominantly favourable weather conditions, with aboveaverage rainfall in July. In most of the country, the yield outlook for summer crops exceeds the 5-year average by more than 10%. The southern-central oblasts experienced below-average rainfall in August, but this did not cause severe damage to summer crops.

Winter and spring cereals benefited from favourable spring weather conditions. The yield forecasts for wheat and winter barley remain unchanged, i.e., above average in most of the country. Spring barley benefited from abundant rainfall during grain filling, leading to an upward revision in yield forecasts for all oblasts. The favourable conditions in July boosted the development of summer crops. Yield forecasts were revised upwards for most of the country, except for the southern and western oblasts. However, the summer crop area is significantly reduced compared with the period before Russia's invasion in Ukraine, particularly in oblasts located in the conflict zones.

Despite the forecast increase in yield by 19%, we expect that the production of grain maize at national level will be reduced by 3% compared to the 2017-2021 average. The areas cultivated with sunflowers and soybeans were less affected than maize, and our production forecast increased to 17% (sunflowers) and 30% (soybeans) above the pre-war average. We estimate that of the total production of summer crops 3% of grain maize, 17% of sunflowers, and 6% of soybeans remain in occupied territory.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023 | period: 2023-09 | section: Meteorological overview
text: Warmer-than-usual conditions prevailed in the country, particularly in western parts and during August. A drier-thanusual start to the summer (June) was followed by a wetter-than-usual July; and then a drier-than-usual August, particularly in the second half of the month in eastern and central regions.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023 | period: 2023-09 | section: June
text:
- Drier-than-usual conditions were observed in parts of eastern Ukraine (Luhans’ka, Donets’ka) and most of central Ukraine, with rainfall only 0-50% of the long-term average (LTA) in most of Cherkas’ka, parts of Vinnyts’ka, Kirovohrads’ka and Mykolayivs’ka, and in the northern and southernmost parts of Odes’ka oblast.

- Warmer-than-usual conditions, with daily average temperatures exceeding the LTA by between 0.5 °C and 2 °C, were observed in most of Vinnyts’ka, as well as in southern Zhytomyrs’ka and parts of Cherkas’ka, Kirovohrads’ka, Mikolayivs’ka and Odes’ka oblasts. Colder-than-usual conditions, with daily average temperatures down to between 0.5 °C and 2 °C below the LTA, were observed in eastern Ukraine and in parts of L’vivs’ka, Ivano-Frankivs’ka and Zakarpats’ka oblasts in the west.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023 | period: 2023-09 | section: July
text:
- Wetter-than-usual conditions were observed in most of the country, with rainfall exceeding the LTA by 100% and more in central (Kyyvs’ka, Cherkas’ka), eastern (Kharkivs’ka, Dnipropetrovs’ka, Zaporiz’ka) and southern

(Mikolayivs’ka, Odes’ka, Krym) Ukraine. Drier-than-usual conditions prevailed in eastern Ukraine (Luhans’ka and Donets’ka).

- Warmer-than-usual conditions prevailed in most of western and southern Ukraine. Colder-than-usual conditions were observed in parts of northern (Chernihivs’ka, Sums’ka, Kyyivs’ka, Poltavs’ka) and eastern (Donets’ka) regions of the country.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023 | period: 2023-09 | section: August
text:
- Drier-than-usual conditions were observed in eastern Ukraine (parts of Luhans’ka, Donets’ka, most of Zaporiz’ka and parts of Khersons’ka and Krym oblasts) and in central Ukraine (Zhytomyrs’ka, Kyyivs’ka, southern Chernihivs’ka, Cherkas’ka, Vinnyts’ka and parts of Khmel’nyts’ka and Odes’ka oblasts), and extended across most of the country in the second half of August. Wetter-than-usual conditions, with rainfall exceeding the LTA by more than 100%, were observed in northern central Ukraine (Sums’ka, Poltavs’ka) in the first half of August.

- Warmer-than-usual conditions were observed across the country, with average daily temperatures exceeding the LTA by between 0.5 °C and 2 °C in most of eastern Ukraine, and up to 4 °C in western Ukraine.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023

section: Crop growth conditions Winter and spring crops
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023 | period: 2023-09 | section: Crop growth conditions Winter and spring crops
text:
Favourable spring weather conditions boosted the development of winter and spring crops, with June providing ideal conditions for growth. However, heavy rainfall in July delayed harvesting and potentially affected grain quality, while dry conditions in August hindered rapeseed sowing.

Winter and spring crops benefited from favourable spring conditions, with overall mild temperatures that boosted their development. Late spring was drier than usual in the north-western half of Ukraine, which was beneficial during the flowering stage. Weather conditions in June allowed steady growth and development of winter crops through the grain-filling stage, without them experiencing water stress or temperature-related stress. As phenological development followed a seasonal course, harvesting of winter crops started in late June / early July. However, substantial rainfall between 6 and 9 July in a large part of the country (to the west of a band expanding from Vinnyts'ka and Odes’ka to Chernihivs'ka and Kharkivs'ka) delayed the start or impeded the progress of harvesting. Later in July, frequent rains additionally delayed the progress of harvesting (by a week at national level) compared to 2022. Dry weather conditions in August allowed the work to catch up and harvesting was completed in late August. The wet conditions in July may have had an adverse impact on grain quality, which remains to be confirmed. The yield forecasts for rapeseed, winter wheat and winter barley remain unchanged from the June edition of the Bulletin, i.e. above the trend throughout the country except in north-eastern parts (Kharkivs'ka). Spring barley, which is cultivated more in the north-east, benefited from abundant rainfall during grain filling, and the yield forecasts were revised upwards for all oblasts. The dry conditions in most of the country starting in mid- August caused topsoils to become very dry, resulting in delays to the rapeseed sowing campaign. It is most likely that the 10-40 mm of rainfall in late August and early September, in the eastern half of the country, has been sufficient for favourable emergence conditions; however, more rain would be beneficial.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023 | period: 2023-09 | section: Summer crops
text:
Differences between the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) cumulated from 1 to 31 August 2023 and the medium-term average (MTA, 2013-2022) for the same periods, in arable land areas.

Summer crop sowings were delayed compared to the previous season, due to abundant spring rainfall. Higherthan-usual temperatures, which persisted until mid-June, accelerated crop development. Maize and sunflowers benefited from the overall wetter-than-usual summer conditions, despite occasional rainfall deficits in June and August in southern regions. High yields are expected in major production areas.

Grain maize, mostly cultivated in the central and northernmost parts of Ukraine, benefited from aboveaverage precipitation from June to August. Most fields did not experience water stress during the season. In June and July, temperatures were generally in line with the LTA (slightly below average in the eastern part of the country), which was beneficial for vegetative development and flowering. In August, rainfed crops in areas that were affected by high temperatures combined with rainfall deficits (such as in Vinnyts’ka, Zhytomyrs’ka and Kyyvs’ka), presented an early onset of ripening, thus reducing the potential for very high yields under rainfed cultivation.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023 | period: 2023-09 | section: Summer crops
text:
Sunflower production is concentrated in the eastern and south-eastern regions of the country, which experienced no long dry period until mid-August. This was particularly true in Dnipropetrovs'ka, where rainfall exceeded the LTA by 15% during the 3-month period. Starting in mid- August, a significant rain deficit caused an early onset of leaf senescence. Additionally, the ongoing war in the frontline regions has led to a significant reduction in cultivated areas. It is worth noting that the strongly positive anomaly observed in the remote sensing map for August in some areas (Khersons'ka, Zaporiz’ka, Donets’ka, Kharkivs’ka) is closely related to spontaneous vegetation growth associated with the increasing abandonment of land due to the current and past effects of the war (see Appendix 2). Abandoned land tends to exhibit late starts in canopy development in spring (due to lack of management, as reported in the March Bulletin) and high biomass during summer due to favourable weather conditions, in particular in areas which in a normal season have a high share of ripening and harvested winter crops around this time.

Soybeans are primarily grown in the western half of Ukraine. The oblasts of Khmel’nyts’ka, Zhytomyrs’ka and Vinnyts’ka experienced average rainfall, temperature and radiation levels, which were favourable for soybean cultivation. However, starting in the second dekad of August, these regions observed 2 weeks with less than 5 mm of rainfall, leading to crop senescence and reduced grain filling, and diminishing the high yield potential.

At the national level, our yield forecast for the three summer crops exceeds historical trends, with increases above the 5-year average for grain maize (+20%), sunflowers (+20%), and soybean (+7%). This translates to respectively 29%, 12%, and 7% increase in yields compared to the yields observed in 2022.

section: Appendix Appendix 1: Summer crop area estimates
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023 | period: 2023-09 | section: Appendix Appendix 1: Summer crop area estimates
text:
Figure 1. Comparison of KPI remote sensing based areas estimate of summer crops as compared to Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food (MAPF) of Ukraine for 2023 (left) and 2021 (right).

The Kyiv Polytechnic Institute (KPI) map used for our estimates of the area of summer crops in nongovernment-controlled oblasts was released on 10 July 2023, and is based on Copernicus Sentinel-1 and Sentinel- 2 data up to the end of June. While the winter crop estimates demonstrate high reliability (e.g., rapeseed with an accuracy1 of 0.97), the accuracy of the estimates of summer crops areas is lower. When considered as a single class, summer crops are correctly distinguished from other crops (accuracy of 0.93).; however, the differentiation of the three major summer crops (grain maize, sunflower, and soybean) is not sufficiently accurate (accuracies ranging from 0.62 to 0.83) to serve as a basis for area monitoring. The figure 1-left presents the 2023 KPI summer crop estimates for government-controlled oblasts in comparison to the figures provided by the Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food (MAPF) of Ukraine. It demonstrates an overall good match. However, two oblasts, Dnipropetrovs'ka and Kharkivs'ka, distinctly

A similar comparative analysis using the 2021 KPI map, conducted on consolidated official statistics, reveals an excellent correlation with minimal bias (figure 1-right). This reinforces the trust in the high quality of the 2023 KPI map for assessing summer crop areas. For the four occupied oblasts (Luhans'ka, Donets'ka, Khersons'ka, Zaporiz'ka), we utilized the 2023 KPI estimates of summer crops, which were unbiased based on the regression calculated using other oblasts except for Dnipropetrovs'ka and Kharkivs'ka. header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023 | period: 2023-09 | section: Appendix 2: Detection of abandoned land
text:
Figure 2. Percentage of abandoned land at village level in 2023 with respect to arable land in 2021 (source: Kyiv

Polytechnic Institute).

Based on evidence from high-resolution Copernicus Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery, up to 4.7 Mha of agricultural land has been abandoned in 2023 (source: Kyiv Polytechnic Institute). Abandoned land is mostly concentrated along the current and past conflict zone. Because of sufficient rainfall, abandoned land appears as fully vegetated due to extensive weed cover. Abandonment is mostly attributed to inaccessibility and the extensive presence of mines and unexploded ordnance. Note that the conflict area is also marked with high values in the MODIS NDVI mosaic (see section on crop canopy conditions). The impact of the Kakhovka dam break on 6 June 2023 is clearly reflected in abandonment of areas that were flooded downstream in south-western Khersons’ka oblast. A somewhat surprising effect is visible on the Crimean Peninsula, which is currently not affected by large-scale military activities. The abandonment here is likely triggered by the lack of irrigation water linked to the destruction of the Kakhovka dam.

section: Appendix 3: Comparison of wheat area, production and yield 2023 forecasts for government-controlled areas
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2023 | period: 2023-09 | section: Appendix 3: Comparison of wheat area, production and yield 2023 forecasts for government-controlled areas
text:
Figure 3. The three graphs at the top show the 2023 forecasts for production (left), yield (centre) and area (right) of wheat in the government-controlled areas in Ukraine, according to assessments by different entities at several dates during the season. The three graphs at the bottom show the actual amount of wheat harvested (left), the average yield of the area harvested (centre) and the area harvested (right) during the course of the wheat harvesting campaign, as reported by the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food (MAPF). The final values of the 2023 MAPF harvest reports are shown as dotted horizontal lines in the graphs at the top.

In the earliest assessments, most distinctly until May, the JRC MARS production and yield forecasts clearly stand out by being substantially higher than the forecasts from the other entities, but well in line with the final figures. According to JRC MARS, the high forecasts are based on predominantly favourable weather conditions in the important wheat production areas in the country, and fairto-good crop conditions as inferred from remote sensing imagery. These observations suggest that, despite the constraints imposed by the war, overall crop management can be expected to be adequate in most of the areas sown to wheat. The other sources (e.g. Agritel) confirmed the overall favourable weather and crop conditions, but assumed a strong negative effect of the ongoing war on final yields and production.

In June, based on continued favourable conditions, JRC MARS revised its yield forecast further up, but revised the area estimate downwards, mainly due to a much higherthan-usual share of rapeseed, which could be distinguished from the other winter crops during flowering, and KPI reports on extensive land abandonment (see also Appendix 2). This resulted in a moderate increase in the JRC MARS production forecast. The majority of the other entities sharply increased their production estimates only after the first actual harvesting figures were published in July by the Ukrainian MAPF2. NASA Harvest is one of the other entities known to integrate high resolution Earth observation in their analysis, resulting in close agreement with the final figures, but only at the onset of harvest.
