section: June 2024 Below average yield outlook for winter crops
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2024 | period: 2024-06 | section: June 2024 Below average yield outlook for winter crops
text:
While weather conditions were overall positive until April, a rain deficit in May followed by a heatwave in June adversely affected the yield potential for winter crops. The yield forecast is reduced compared to 2023 but remains close to the 5-year average. Production forecasts are below last year’s level for all grains except soybeans.

Following an overall warm winter, spring weather was marked by contrasts. A persistent rain deficit in the east led to very poor crop conditions, while favourable conditions prevailed in the west until April. In May, a significant rain deficit impacted winter crops during flowering across the country; and in June, a heatwave in the east threatened grain filling for cereals. Field abandonment continues to be observed in several parts of the country. For Ukraine as a whole, there is a decrease in the area of winter cereals compared to last year, particularly affecting oblasts close to the front line and in the northeast near the Russian border. The rapeseed area has slightly decreased compared to 2023. The areas for grain maize and sunflower remained stable, while soybean has increased.

Compared with last year, at the country level, our forecast for grain production is reduced for all crops (except for soybean) due to decreases in both area and yields. The production for wheat is forecast at 20.7 MT (down 25% compared to 2023), and for winter barley at 2.9 MT (down 12%), with the caveat that 12.5% of the production of these cereals remains in oblasts under Russian occupation. Rapeseed production is forecast to be reduced by 12% compared to 2023, mostly due to a negative yield outlook in the south of the country. Our yield forecasts for summer crops currently follow the 5-year average.

Overall, warmer-than-usual conditions were observed in most of Ukraine from late autumn to spring. However, substantial temperature swings occurred during this period, which brought frequent thaws followed by cold snaps. Spring was much warmer than average, particularly the last dekad of May and early June. Drier-than-usual conditions in southern regions in October were interrupted by wetter-than-usual November and January, but reoccurred since then, particularly in southern and eastern regions. Most regions were drier-than-usual in May and early June.

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2024 | period: 2024-06 | section: Winter crops
text:
Mixed weather conditions since the beginning of the season have resulted in suboptimal development of winter cereals, particularly in the eastern and southern oblasts. Consequently, yield potentials were reduced, and the yield forecasts at national level are below the historical trend.

The remote sensing map above reflects predominantly winter crop conditions because summer crops, for which the season just started, contribute minimally to the variation in fAPAR at this point in time. In the western and northern regions of the country, the map indicates overall above-average biomass accumulation, which is mainly due to an early onset of regrowth after the winter. However, most other parts of the country (excluding Odes’ka and Mykolayivs'ka), present a negative anomaly. The warmer-than-usual conditions at the start of the season for wintercrops, in October and November, were favorable for sowing of winter cereals. However, in the south (Odes’ka), the significantly drier-than-usual conditions resulted in poorly developed stands.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2024

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2024 | period: 2024-06 | section: Winter crops
text:
The winter was significantly warmer than usual, and winter crops were not exposed to any severe cold spells. These favourable conditions led to above-average leaf area at the end of the winter in most of the country, except in the southern oblasts such as Odes’ka, where the water deficit persisted until mid-March. Since the beginning of March, continuing mild temperatures allowed winter crops to emerge from dormancy and to restart growth early, supported by regular rainfall until the end of April. Only the eastern oblasts experienced significant water deficits (from early- March to mid-April) that hampered crop growth and development. In the south (mostly, Odes’ka and Mykolayivs'ka), the abundant rain at the end of March mitigated the adverse effects of the dry winter. Cereals are growing at average to above average rates in these two oblasts, but rapeseed was severely impacted by the dry conditions during winter. This is reflected in a decrease in rapeseed detection from remote sensing (see appendix A). In May, a significant and prolonged rain deficit adversely affected the cereals during flowering and the grain filling phase. In early June, the resurgence of rainfall in the western half of the country mitigated the impacts, particularly in the north, where plant senescence had not yet commenced. Meanwhile, the eastern half of the country experienced a substantial number of consecutive hot days, with maximum temperatures exceeding 30 degrees Celsius. This heatwave which continued after the review period is expected to affect the grain filling process of cereal crops. Given the contrastful weather conditions depicted above, the yield outlook for winter crops varies from fairly positive in the west and north to strongly negative in the east. In Luhans’ka and Donets’ka, the yield forecast is close to the lowest of the past 5 years. At the national level, our forecast for the three winter crops remains below the historical trend for the government-controlled areas and the country as a whole. It is worth noting that these forecasts consider a disruption of the positive yield trend that the country experienced over the past 20 years due to agrotechnological developments.

In the context of the war, we considered a pause in this trend due to the logistical and financial difficulties faced by Ukrainian farmers..

section: Spring and summer crops Spring barley
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2024 | period: 2024-06 | section: Spring and summer crops Spring barley
text: In late February, the sowing campaign of spring barley started in southern Ukraine; sooner than usual thanks to mild temperatures of late winter. Sowing progress was initially hampered by frequent rains, but got to full swing after 20 March. Above-average temperatures and sparse rain supported the good pace of the sowing campaign, and by the end of April it was concluded all over Ukraine, one to two weeks earlier than usual. Warmer-than-usual temperatures in March and April resulted in above-average phenological development, leaf area expansion and biomass accumulation. Crop water supply was adequate in the western and central regions. However, in eastern parts of the country (e.g. Kharkivs’ka, Donets’ka, Luhans’ka), where rainfall was well below the LTA, the high temperatures of in June and low soil moisture contents can compromise the yield formation during the flowering and grain filling period.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2024

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2024 | period: 2024-06 | section: Sunflowers, grain maize and soybeans
text:
Abundant precipitation in late March, early April somewhat hampered the field preparations for summer crops. The sowing of sunflower started in the first dekad of April, while maize and soybean sowing began just in the second dekad of April in the southernmost areas. Progress of sowing was hampered until late April by frequent and

1 https://minagro.gov.ua/map considerable rainfall events. However, reports from early May indicate a marked uptick in the pace of sowing, which persisted through the end of May. (e.g. Sums’ka). Planting efforts, particularly for soybeans, extended into June. It is anticipated that all planting will be concluded by mid-June. According to the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food, the soybean area in the government-controlled areas presents (as reported on 06 June, 2024 1) an increase compared with the 2023 crop season. April's unusually warm temperatures offered optimal conditions for sprouting, emergence and accelerated initial development of summer crops. However, the cold period of mid-May slowed down the development of early sown summer crops and delayed the emergence of those sown later. Around 10 May, frosts events occurred, mainly in the north-eastern regions, causing local damage to the seedlings of maize and sunflower, but also negatively affecting spring barley. This delay in crop development lessened towards late May and early June, thanks to higher-than-average temperatures. Overall, canopy expansion and leaf area index of summer crops are at an average level. However, the rainfall deficit in the east raises concerns regarding a possible summer drought. The yield forecast for summer crops currently follows the 5-year average, however there is a risk of negative impacts due to unfavourable dry and hot conditions during summer primarily in the eastern regions..

section: Appendix Crop area and crop phenology – an analysis using Copernicus Sentinel-2 data A- Winter and spring crops area
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2024 | period: 2024-06 | section: Appendix Crop area and crop phenology – an analysis using Copernicus Sentinel-2 data A- Winter and spring crops area
text:
The area for winter crops in government-controlled areas was deduced from the sowing reports delivered by the Ministry of Agriculture as of the end of December. From these reports, we obtained the sown areas for winter wheat, winter barley, and rapeseed. However, these numbers did not entirely match the press release from the Ministry dated April 172. This was particularly the case for the rapeseed area, which in the sowing report was underestimated by 20%. We adjusted the per-oblast areas for rapeseed accordingly, to be in line with the information of the more recently published press release. Using the same methodology as in last year’s June edition of the Ukraine bulletin3, we estimated the identified the areas of winter and spring crops based on the analysis of time series of Sentinel-2 imagery. This method was applied to all oblasts of Ukraine, but only the results for the occupied oblasts are reported in the Bulletin. First, we applied a spectral threshold on the NDVI maximum value composite from February to end of May to identify pixels with winter and spring crops; then, rapeseed was distinguished from these crops, using a spectral threshold on the yellow index maximum value composite show the overall match between the end-of-campaign sowing progress reports and the remote sensing based estimates for both winter and spring crops and rapeseed. In the case of rapeseed, the most distinct discrepancies are for

Odes'ka and Mykolayivs'ka. In both oblasts the reported area is much larger than the areas inferred from the satellite-based yellow index composites. We attribute this discrepancy to the dry conditions that prevailed until the end of April in these regions, which negatively affected rapeseed flowering. The areas of winter cereals were calculated by subtracting the rapeseed areas from the total areas of winter crops. These outputs were then distributed among individual crops according to the 5-year average shares for winter wheat, winter barley, and spring barley.

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2024 | period: 2024-06 | section: B- LAI crop-specific analysis
text:
We derived the leaf area index (LAI) profiles for winter cereal and rapeseed parcels identified using the method described in Appendix A. We then assessed the growth patterns of these crops by comparing them with parcels represented in crop maps from preceding years from the same oblast. Utilizing high-resolution Sentinel-2 imagery, this approach offers a notable improvement over the method normally employed in the Bulletin, which is based on non-crop-specific MODIS data. At the regional level, we aggregated the LAI profiles for various parcels of winter cereals and winter rapeseed. The 2024 time series ends at varying dates for different regions, due to the variability in cloud cover and the availability of Sentinel-2 observations.

Ukraine, September 2024
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2024

section: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook Crop monitoring European neighbourhood Ukraine September 2024 Severe drought led to below-average yield outlook for summer crops
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2024 | period: 2024-09 | section: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook Crop monitoring European neighbourhood Ukraine September 2024 Severe drought led to below-average yield outlook for summer crops
text:
Throughout the summer of 2024, Ukraine experienced unusually dry conditions. While yields of winter and spring crops remained close to the 5-year average, the outlook for summer crops is below average, but without reaching a historical low.

Spring weather conditions were generally favourable in most of the country. However, as of June, temperatures consistently exceeded the long-term average, and an intense drought affected two-thirds of the country from late June to early September. These drought conditions had limited impacts on winter crop yields, as the season was about to end. However, they severely affected summer crops in all oblasts east of Kyyivs'ka. The non-government controlled areas experienced a significant increase in abandoned land, leading to a substantial decrease in cultivated areas compared to last year. In the rest of the country, the total area of arable land was preserved. Wheat, barley, rapeseed, grain maize, and sunflower areas decreased compared to 2023, while the soybean area continued its positive trend.

The production of wheat and barley is significantly below the 5-year average and 2023, primarily due to reduced harvest areas. Both grain maize and sunflower production suffered from reduced yields and areas, whereas soybean production is expected to increase due to the expansion of sown areas. The production in Russian-occupied territories was substantially reduced due to the increase in abandoned land and the strong yield reduction. We estimate that of the total production of summer crops, 1% of grain maize, 13% of sunflowers, and 2% of soybeans remain in non-government controlled areas.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2024

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2024 | period: 2024-09 | section: Meteorological overview
text:
Distinctly warmer-than-usual conditions prevailed in all of Ukraine during the summer months. Marked positive temperature anomalies characterised northern and western regions in the first half of July and the second half of August, and intensified in early September. Whereas a rainfall surplus was observed mainly in northern central regions in June and parts of western regions in early July, much drier-than-usual conditions developed and persisted in central and eastern regions in July, and in most of Ukraine in August.

The weather synthesis map represents a summary of the most distinct weather anomalies during the reporting period (1 June to 10 September 2024) compared with the 1991–2023 long-term average (LTA) for the same period. Temperature surplus and rainfall deficit are unusual absolute and relative deviations from the LTA, considering the reporting period as a whole. Hot spells are 5-day periods with temperatures above the 90th percentile of the years since 1991. The single-indicator maps below provide further context on each type of event.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2024

- Wetter-than-usual conditions in western regions and central northern regions, with cumulative precipitation mostly between 100% and 150% above the LTA; more than 150% above the LTA in Chernihivs’ka and locally in Sums’ka.

Near-average conditions in L’vivs’ka,

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2024 | period: 2024-09 | section: Weather forecast 11–20 September
text:
- With the exception of Zakarpats’ka, where near-average daily temperatures are forecast, distinct positive temperature anomalies relative to the LTA are forecast for most regions, from up to 2 °C above the LTA in southern Odes’ka and south-western regions (Chernivets’ka, Ivano-Frankivs’ka, L’vivs’ka, Ternopil’s’ka, southern Khmel’nyts’ka) to 6 °C or more in north-eastern regions (Chernihivs’ka, Sums’ka, Kharkivs’ka, Luhans’ka).

- Dry conditions (cumulative precipitation of up to 3 mm) are forecast for eastern regions (Sums’ka, Kharkivs’ka, Luhans’ka, Donets’ka, Zaporiz’ka, and parts of Khersons’ka and Krym). Wet conditions (cumulative precipitation of more than 90 mm) are forecast for southern and south-western regions (Ivano-frankivs’ka, Chernivets’ka, Ternopil’s’ka, Khmel’nyts’ka, Vinnytis’ka and Odes’ka). Cumulative precipitation of more than 100 mm is forecast in the regions bordering Moldova and in parts of Khmel’nyts’ka, Ternopil’s’ka and Ivano-frankivs’ka.

section: Crop growth conditions Winter and spring crops
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2024 | period: 2024-09 | section: Crop growth conditions Winter and spring crops
text:
Warmer-than-usual weather resulted in accelerated crop development and led to early harvests. In the eastern oblasts, pronounced soil moisture deficits and heatwaves negatively affected soft wheat during the grain-filling period. Weather conditions in the central and western oblasts were more favourable for yield formation. Yield forecasts for winter crops were maintained. The forecast for spring barley was revised slightly downwards.

As reported in the June edition of this bulletin, significant precipitation at the beginning of June mitigated any negative impacts of the prevailing water deficit in most of Ukraine, particularly in the north, but was insufficient to benefit winter crops in the east, where heatwaves and continued inadequate water supply caused severe losses to the yield potential. This year, winter wheat, winter barley and rapeseed presented exceptionally accelerated phenological development; therefore, the harvest started around mid June in the southernmost regions. In the last dekad of June and in July, dry and hot weather in the central and eastern regions provided favourable conditions for harvesting. In the western regions (e.g. Rivnens’ka, Khmelnyts'ka and Ternopil's'ka), harvesting was hampered by periods of abundant rainfall. However, overall progress of harvesting was fast, and it was practically concluded by 22 August, with low harvest losses and little negative impact on grain quality. We maintain our yield forecasts for winter crops as published in the June edition of this bulletin. Meanwhile, we have updated the area statistics in accordance with the harvest report of the Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food of Ukraine (instead of the sowing report). Consequently, the area and production figures reported here are different from the figures reported in June. Spring barley benefited from early sowing thanks to mild spring temperatures. Favourable conditions continued to prevail in the western and central regions, whereas in the eastern production regions, the inadequate water supply and hot temperatures compromised the yield outlook. On the balance, our spring barley yield forecast is slightly above the 5-year average. The harvest of spring barley started in late June and progressed well except during the rainy periods in the west. The harvest was completed in late August.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2024

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2024 | period: 2024-09 | section: Summer crops
text:
Differences between the fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (fAPAR) cumulated from 1 to 10 September 2024 and the medium-term average (MTA, 2014-2023) for the same periods, in arable land areas.

Spring weather conditions were generally favourable in two thirds of the country, with the exception of the eastern part, where rainfall deficits persisted from March onwards. Beginning in June, temperatures persistently surpassed the LTA, and an intense drought affected most of the country from late June to early September, significantly affecting the outlook for summer crops.

Grain maize sowing occurred at a normal pace, and was concluded by the end of May. Favourable weather conditions prevailed during the early development stage in western and most central oblasts. However, in the eastern half of the country (including Poltavs'ka and Cherkas'ka), the intensifying rainfall deficit had a strong impact on maize, particularly in the south-east
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2024

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2024 | period: 2024-09 | section: Summer crops
text:
(Khersons’ka and Zaporiz'ka). Conversely, in western and northern areas (e.g. Chernihivs'ka), adequate water supply up to mid August created favourable conditions for grain maize. Although the persistently positive temperature anomaly was detrimental to the overall yield potential, the absence of extreme maximum temperatures (they rarely exceeded 36 °C) mitigated the temperature's impact on yields. Grain maize harvesting commenced earlier than usual, especially in drought-affected parcels in southern oblasts. Sunflower production in Ukraine occurs predominantly in the eastern and south-eastern regions, which were severely affected by the extremely dry conditions prevailing in July and August. Among the major sunflowerproducing oblasts, only Vinnyts'ka (in the central west) has received rainfall close to the LTA since June. The drought had a profound impact on sunflower crops, which are cultivated without irrigation systems in Ukraine. As a result, harvesting began earlier than usual in the eastern regions, driven by accelerated phenology. Soybeans is mostly cultivated in the western half of the country, which was less affected by the drought. The higher-than-normal temperatures were overall negative for crop development. The rain deficit in August in almost all of the country brought forward the senescence phase and shortened the grain-filling phase. It is worth noting that, in the oblast of Khersons’ka, historically a big producer of soybean under irrigation, the drought was also associated with irrigation failure, certainly due to the destruction of the Kakhovka dam in 2023. At the national level, the harvest has started earlier than usual, and field reports sustain an above-average outlook, except in southern and eastern oblasts. Our yield forecast at the national level for the three summer crops is below the 5-year average for grain maize (– 8%) and sunflowers (– 7%), and just above the 5-year average for soybean (+ 1%). This translates to decreases in yields compared with the yields observed in 2023, by 17% for grain maize, 9% for sunflowers and 9% for soybean.

text: A comparison (Figure 1) was made between the June 2024 forecast for soft wheat and rapeseed reported in the JRC MARS Bulletin and the figures of the final harvest reports provided by the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food (MAPF). For soft wheat, at the national level, the June JRC MARS forecast for soft wheat was 0.33 t/ha (6.5%) lower than the yield derived from the August harvest report. text: in 2024 remains largely concentrated in and along the conflict zone, where land abandonment has intensified. This intensification is particularly pronounced in nongovernment-controlled areas, and in eastern parts of Dnipropetrovs’ka and Kharkivs’ka. In other areas, the increase in abandoned land from 2023 to 2024 has been limited; and in some areas there has been a decrease in abandoned land (e.g. Odes’ka, western Khersons’ka), suggesting that Ukrainian farmers are making concerted efforts to maintain grain production.

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2024 | period: 2024-09 | section: C- LAI crop-specific analysis
text:
Leaf area index (LAI) profiles for land parcels with summer crops were derived from Copernicus Sentinel-2 remote sensing data, utilising the Kyiv Polytechnic Institute’s

2019–2024 crop classification map (Figure 3). Although the 2024 map, processed in July, is not final, a comparison with ground samples has demonstrated its high level of accuracy. The growth patterns of summer crops were assessed by drawing comparisons with patterns in parcels from the same oblast in crop maps from previous years. The LAI for parcels with the three monitored summer crops (grain maize, sunflower and soybean) were aggregated at the regional level to provide a comprehensive overview. This approach uses highresolution Sentinel-2 imagery, providing a significant improvement with respect to the standard method employed in the Bulletin, which relies on non-crop-specific

MODIS data. This analysis yields more accurate remote sensing data, which enhances the accuracy of yield predictions at the oblast level.

Figure 1: Comparison between the June 2024 forecast for soft wheat and rapeseed reported in the JRC MARS Bulletin and the figures of the final harvest reports provided by the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food (MAPF).

Figure 2: Percentage of abandoned land at village level in 2023 and 2024 with respect to total land area (source: Kyiv Polytechnic Institute).

Figure 3: Sentinel-2-based Leaf area index (LAI) profiles for three summer crops in selected producing oblasts. Time series are extracted for parcels identified for each crop types and compared to previous years.

JRC MARS Bulletin – Global outlook

Ukraine, June 2025
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025

section: June 2025 Average yield outlook for winter crops, despite strong rainfall deficit in the east
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025 | period: 2025-06 | section: June 2025 Average yield outlook for winter crops, despite strong rainfall deficit in the east
text:
Persistent drier-than-usual weather negatively affected winter cereals in the east, while two cold spells during late spring reduced the yield potential of rapeseed in the west. Elsewhere, predominantly seasonal conditions helped to maintain winter crop yields above the five-year average. Based on remote-sensing-derived area estimates and observed crop conditions, the production outlook for winter cereals is below the five-year average. In contrast, rapeseed production is expected to increase, driven by an expansion in sown area.

A rainfall deficit persisted in the eastern and northernmost oblasts during most of the cropping season, negatively affecting winter cereals. In the western oblasts, late cold spells in spring compromised the flowering and early pod filling of rapeseed. Nonetheless, timely rainfall and belowaverage temperatures in May were beneficial for the final development stages of winter crops, further supported by a positive weather forecast until the end of June. Production forecasts for all winter crops and spring barley are slightly below the five-year average with considerable interregional variability. Field abandonment remains evident, particularly in areas close to the front line of the

Yield forecasts for Ukraine - 16 June 2025 Bulletin war. However, Sentinel-2 analysis indicates a relatively stable area of winter cereals in the government-controlled areas along with a notable increase in rapeseed area, particularly in the southern oblasts. The sowing campaign of summer crops is nearing completion, with a reduction observed in the sown area of grain maize and sunflowers, while the soybean area has increased. Early crop development is reported to be fair, with a good water supply in the western regions, but at risk in the east due to the persistent rainfall deficit. Yield forecasts for summer crops are still in line with the fiveyear average.

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025 | period: 2025-06 | section: Weather Review
text: Drier-than-usual conditions, with cumulative rainfall only 50% of the long-term average (LTA) or less, characterised the east of the country and parts of the westernmost oblasts during most of the crop season, while in other western and central regions winter and late spring precipitation provided a fair water supply. Drier-than-usual conditions are forecast until late June, except in the north. Most of Ukraine experienced a warmer-than-usual winter and early spring, especially in December to January and in March. Whereas February was characterised by colder-than-usual temperatures in all regions, pronounced cold spells occurred in the western oblasts in early April and the first half of May. In early June, temperatures increased to above average across the country, while until late June slightly colder-than-usual temperatures are forecast.

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025 | period: 2025-06 | section: 1.1. Autumn/winter (October 2024 to February 2025)
text:
October

Warmer-than-usual conditions, with average daily temperatures between 0.5 °C and 2 °C above the LTA in most regions and up to 3 °C above the LTA in central and northern oblasts (Sums’ka, western Kharkivs’ka, Poltavs’ka, eastern Cherkas’ka, most of Kirovohrads’ka, western Dnipropetrovs’ka and northern Mykolayivs’ka).

Significantly wetter than usual in central and southern regions, including Odes’ka and southern Zaporiz’ka, with rainfall totals between 100% and 150% (locally more) above the LTA. Drier than usual in eastern regions (Luhans’ka, Donets’ka), with cumulative rainfall only 50% of the LTA or less.

November

Near-normal temperatures in most of the country; slightly colder than usual (1–2 °C below the LTA) in the west (most of Zakarpats’ka) and south (Odes’ka).

Wetter than usual in the north, with cumulative rainfall between 50% and 100% above the LTA, mainly in Sums’ka. Drier than usual in the west (L’vivs’ka, Volyns’ka), south (Odes’ka, parts of Mykolayivs’ka) and east (Zaporiz’ka, Donets’ka), with less than 50% of the LTA.

December

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025 | period: 2025-06 | section: 1.1. Autumn/winter (October 2024 to February 2025)
text:
Warmer-than-usual conditions, with average daily temperatures between 0.5 °C and 2 °C above the LTA in most of Ukraine, and between 2 °C and 3 °C above the LTA in eastern Sums’ka, Kharkivs’ka and neighbouring regions. Wetter than usual, with cumulative precipitation between 50% and 100% above the LTA, in parts of Odes’ka, north-western Mykolayivs’ka and western Kirovhrads’ka, and locally in Cherkas’ka and in the south (Khmel’nyts’ka) and east (Chernivets’ka). Drier than usual, with rainfall totalling 50% of the LTA or less in the westernmost oblasts, the north and north-east, and parts of the south-east.

January

Considerably warmer-than-usual conditions, with average daily temperatures between 4 °C and 5 °C above the LTA in most of the west and up to 6 °C above the LTA in the east.

Significantly drier than usual, with hardly any rainfall in most of Ukraine.

February

Colder-than-usual conditions, with average daily temperatures up to 2 °C below the LTA in most of Ukraine and up to 4 °C below the LTA in parts of southern oblasts (Odeks’ka, Krym) and in the east.

Persistently drier-than-usual conditions in almost all regions, with a rainfall deficit up to 100% of the LTA.

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025 | period: 2025-06 | section: 1.2. Spring (1 March to 10 June 2025)
text:
March

Warmer-than-usual conditions, with average daily temperatures between 2 °C and 4 °C above the LTA in the west, south and east, and up to 5 °C above the LTA in central, northern and north-eastern regions.

Drier-than-usual conditions in most central, southern and eastern regions, with rainfall up to 100% below the LTA; wetter than usual in the west (Zakarpats’ka) and locally in northernmost regions (northern Sums’ka).

April

Slightly warmer than usual, with average daily temperatures between 0.5 °C and 1 °C (locally up to 2 °C) above the LTA in most of Ukraine; near-normal temperatures in central southern regions and south-eastern regions. Cold spells, between 7 and 10 days (up to 20 days in the Carpathian) with minimum daily temperatures below zero, occurred in most western regions and the north (parts of Chernihivs’ka and Sums’ka and parts of Kharkivs’ka and Luhans’ka).

Drier than usual, with a rainfall deficit up to 100% of the LTA in the north-east and central south, and up to 50% in the remaining central and western regions; slightly wetter than usual only in the south-west and most of Krym, where cumulative rainfall exceeded the LTA by up to 150%.

May to 10 June

Colder than usual in the west, with average daily temperatures between 0.5 °C and 2 °C below the LTA; nearseasonal temperatures in the east; and slightly warmer than usual in Luhans’ka, easternmost Kharkivs’ka and northern Donets’ka. A cold spell with freezing temperatures occurred in the first half of May in the agricultural areas of the Carpathian region (Zakarpats’ka, Ivano-frankivs’ka, southern L’vivs’ka), in Rivnens’ka and the neighbouring oblasts.

text: In contrast to previous months, cumulative rainfall from May to early June was up to 150% above the LTA, particularly in western regions (e.g. Vinnyts’ka and parts of Zhytomyrs’ka and Khmel’nyts’ka). Drier-than-usual conditions prevailed in the south (Krym, parts of Khersons’ka) and the north-east (Luhans’ka), with rainfall deficits around 50% (up to 100% in Krym) of the LTA.

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025 | period: 2025-06 | section: 1.3. Weather forecast (11–20 June)
text:
Slightly colder-than-usual conditions are forecast for most of Ukraine, with average daily temperatures between 0.5 °C and 1 °C below the LTA; up to 2 °C below the LTA for part of regions in the north (mainly Zhytomyrs’ka, parts of Sums’ka, Poltavs’ka and Kharkivs’ka, and southern Krym). Near-normal temperatures are forecast in the southern oblasts and parts of western oblasts.

Wetter-than-usual conditions are forecast in the northern and north-eastern oblasts, and in Krym, with cumulative rainfall up to 150% above the LTA. Drier-than-usual conditions are forecast in the west, most of the south and the east, with rainfall deficits up to 100% of the LTA.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025 | period: 2025-06 | section: Crop growth conditions -
text: The map displays the relative differences (in percentages) between the cumulative fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (fAPAR) from 1 April to 10 June 2025 and the medium-term average (MTA, 2015– 2024) for the same period. Positive anomalies (in green) reflect above-average crop biomass, while negative anomalies (in red) reflect below-average biomass or late crop development. fAPAR data are derived from the MODIS sensor (Moderate-resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on-board NASA’s Terra and Aqua satellites.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025 | period: 2025-06 | section: Winter crops
text: Winter crops generally entered winter dormancy in fair condition, despite a relatively delayed sowing campaign in autumn. Since early spring, winter cereals have been facing rainfall deficits, particularly in the east, while, in the west, rapeseed was negatively affected by several cold spells during the reproductive stages. Consequently, the yield potential of winter crops was locally reduced, leading to national yield forecasts that fall below the historical trend for rapeseed and remain around the five-year average for winter cereals.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025 | period: 2025-06 | section: Winter crops
text: Following a dry and warm summer in 2024, the sowing campaign for winter crops started in early September. Field activities accelerated in early October with the onset of rainfall that improved topsoil moisture conditions. Moderate temperatures provided favourable conditions for germination and early crop development. Aboveaverage temperatures in December delayed the onset of winter dormancy but allowed sowing operations to progress at a typical pace. Remote sensing analysis indicates an increase in the area sown with rapeseed, particularly in the southern oblasts, while areas under soft wheat and winter barley declined compared with the fiveyear average (see Appendix A). Winter crops benefited from generally favourable agrometeorological conditions during the winter, with overall warmer-than-usual temperatures. The predominantly drier-than-usual conditions are not expected to have adversely impacted the crops, as their water requirements are minimal during the dormancy period. In addition, winter crops were sufficiently hardened by February, when below-average temperatures occurred. As a result, frost damage was limited. Mild conditions during March permitted an early restart of vegetative growth and supported above-average biomass accumulation across most regions. In the western and central oblasts (from L’vivs’ka to Kirovohrads’ka), winter crops entered spring in good condition and with adequate water supply. In the southern and eastern oblasts (east of Dnipropetrovs’ka), the persistent rainfall deficit reduced available water in the soil and hampered growth. Moderate temperatures in April supported crop development, and biomass accumulation was above average in most regions, reflecting an advance in crop phenology. While limited rainfall maintained winter cereals in good condition in the western oblasts, a cold spell with several nights below 0 °C negatively affected rapeseed in the early flowering stage. Winter cereals were less affected, as crops were still in vegetative stages. In the eastern (Donets’ka, Zaporiz’ka) and some southern (Vinnits’ka, Odes’ka) oblasts, the below-average rainfall further worsened crops’ condition and reduced their yield potential.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025 | period: 2025-06 | section: Winter crops
text: In May, colder-than-usual weather and timely rainfall presented favourable conditions for winter crops during flowering and early grain filling in western Ukraine (e.g. Khmel’nyts’ka, Vinnyts’ka and Kyyivs’ka). However, two more cold spells at the end of April and in early May occurred in Volyns’ka, Rivnens’ka, Ternopils’ka and Khmel’nyts’ka oblasts during rapeseed flowering and the onset of pod formation. The negative impact of the repeated cold spells on rapeseed are reflected in the cropspecific leaf area index (LAI) analysis, with a noticeable difference between rapeseed and cereals (e.g. L’vivs’ka in Appendix B). In the southern and central regions (Odes’ka, Cherkas’ka), the lower-than-average temperatures in May slowed down the advanced crop development and prolonged the productive stages. This prevented crop condition from deteriorating further, and fair yields are currently expected, supported by the favourable weather forecast until end of June. In contrast, the eastern oblasts (Kharkivs’ka, Dnipropetrovs’ka, Zaporiz’ka, Donets’ka and Luhans’ka) have experienced prolonged dry conditions since the start of the cropping season. Rainfall in May arrived too late to significantly boost growth and increase yield expectations for winter crops. Scarce precipitation during key development stages, including flowering, has substantially reduced the yield potential in the east, as shown in the crop-specific time series. Well-below-average yields are expected. In addition, the analysis of the MODIS map (see above) may be biased, as many uncultivated fields – classified as arable land – show above-average biomass accumulation due to natural vegetation or rangeland growth.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025

section: Spring and summer crops Spring barley
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025 | period: 2025-06 | section: Spring and summer crops Spring barley
text: The sowing campaign of spring barley started on time in early March in southern Ukraine. Fieldwork accelerated and progressed well thanks to mild temperatures and sparse rainfall in the last dekad of March and the first week of April, until a cold and wet spell slowed down the sowing. After that, the sowing followed a normal pace and was completed in early May in most regions. The following crop establishment and early development started in dry and sunny conditions. However, from the second dekad of May onwards, development was delayed due to persistently colder-than-usual temperatures. Our crop model simulations point to slightly below-average leaf area expansion and biomass accumulation. Soil moisture content is critically low in the east and south-east due to the long-lasting precipitation deficit since January; rainfall is urgently needed to avoid a further deterioration of the yield potential. In western and central Ukraine, in contrast, spring barley’s yield potential is maintained thanks to an adequate water supply, despite the delayed crop development so far. Below-average yield is currently forecast at country leve.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025 | period: 2025-06 | section: Grain maize, sunflowers and soybeans
text:
Sowing of summer crops started in late March, but progressed only marginally until 15 April due to freezing temperatures, snowfall and abundant precipitation. Drierand warmer-than-usual conditions permitted an acceleration of the sowing of sunflower and grain maize between mid April and mid May, before it slowed down again due to rainfall in the following weeks. Eventually, sowings were almost completed by early June. The soybean sowing campaign started slowly and accelerated in late April, before making up the delay in the first half of May. Sowing was largely completed by the end of May. According to the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food (MAPF) sowing report 1, the sunflower sown area

1 https://minagro.gov.ua/map decreased in the government-controlled areas compared with previous years, while the soybean sown area increased considerably. The warmer-than-usual conditions in the second half of April provided favourable conditions for the germination and early development of summer crops. However, colderthan-usual conditions prevailing from mid May resulted in a temperature accumulation deficit, particularly in the western regions. For early-sown summer crops, this led to delayed development, while late-sown crops suffered from prolonged and delayed emergence. Above-average daily temperatures in early June allowed partial catchingup and boosted the vegetative development of the summer crops. Our crop model simulations indicate below-average biomass accumulation and canopy expansion, confirming that phenological development is still delayed. As of early June, soil moisture is estimated to be sufficient or favourable in the west and centre, but in considerable deficit in the east and south (Luhans’ka, Donets’ka, Zaporiz’ka, Dnipropetrovs’ka, Khersons’ka and Mykolayivs’ka), putting grain maize in particular at risk, if the dry conditions continue during summer. Our yield forecasts for summer crops are currently in line with the five-year average.

section: Appendix Crop area and crop phenology: an analysis using Copernicus Sentinel-2 data A- Crops area estimates
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025 | period: 2025-06 | section: Appendix Crop area and crop phenology: an analysis using Copernicus Sentinel-2 data A- Crops area estimates
text: The area for winter crops was derived from the analysis of a crop type map produced by the Kyiv Polytechnic Institute (KPI). It is based on machine learning techniques (a combination of multilayer perceptron and random forest) applied to combined monthly cloud-free Copernicus Sentinel-2 mosaics and 15-day Sentinel-1 composites. The methodology has been adapted this year to run on the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem cloud platform and tailored to the delivery of a winter crop map at the end of May using EO data up to 20 May. Extending the time series until August will result in a complete crop map in early September. The KPI method is supported by seasonal ground observations collected in April/May for recognisable winter crops and in June for summer crops. As an extension to the standard field data collection, the KPI was tasked in 2025 to provide separate observations for winter wheat and winter barley. In previous years, these two crops were bundled as ‘winter cereals’ for the May crop map. The labelled data were used in the machine learning model and led to reasonable separation of the two winter cereal types. However, the KPI noted the difficulty in separating winter barley from spring barley during ground data collection, especially where the latter had already emerged. Therefore, we applied split coefficient factors to disaggregate the total barley area from the crop type map. The coefficients are computed from the sowing reports delivered by the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food (MAPF). This applied only to governmentcontrolled areas. For the four non-government-controlled oblasts, the split coefficient factors were derived from pre-war (2021) official statistics. Figure 1 shows the matching between the sowing reports delivered by the MAPF as of the end of December 2024 and the 2025 MARS area estimates for winter crops and spring barley. Rapeseed numbers display that there is good agreement between MAPF and EO-based estimates. An overestimate in Odes’ka oblast is visible. The summer crop areas were derived from the sowing reports of the MAPF (last updated on 12 June 2025).

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2025 | period: 2025-06 | section: B- LAI crop-specific analysis
text:
We derived the Leaf area index (LAI) and Fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (FAPAR) profiles for winter cereal and rapeseed parcels identified using the crop type map described in Appendix A. We then assessed the growth patterns of these crops by comparing them with parcels represented on crop maps from preceding years from the same oblast (Figure 2). Utilising high-resolution Sentinel-2 imagery, this approach offers a notable improvement over the method normally employed in the bulletin, which is based on non-crop-specific MODIS data.

Figure 1: Comparison of winter crops area from MAPF sowing reports and Sentinel-2 estimates.

section: September 2025 Contrasting yield outlooks for summer crops
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025 | period: 2025-09 | section: September 2025 Contrasting yield outlooks for summer crops
text:
Ukraine experienced unusually dry conditions in summer in the southern and eastern oblasts, leading to well belowaverage yields for summer crops there. In contrast, an adequate water supply and the absence of severe heat stress supported a positive yield outlook in the northern and western regions, despite delayed development. A dry start to the summer of 2025 negatively affected the final stages of winter crop development in the central oblasts. In the west, the harvesting campaign was hampered by excessive rainfall in July, which reduced the quality of both grains and rapeseed. Altogether, winter crop yield expectations were slightly below average. While production forecasts for wheat and rapeseed are above the five-year average, thanks to an increased sown area, barley production is expected to fall below average, as the area has been considerably reduced. During most of summer, a rainfall deficit persisted in the eastern and southern oblasts, negatively affecting grain maize, sunflower and soybean. By contrast, the northern and western oblasts profited from an adequate soil moisture, maintaining summer crop yield potential despite delayed development from late sowing and emergence.

Yield forecasts for Ukraine - 15 September 2025 Bulletin

At the national level, grain maize and soybean yields are forecast to be above the five-year average. Soybean production has been further supported by an expansion in cultivated area, while a limited reduction in maize area has not been sufficient to offset the expected yield gains, resulting in production estimates that are still above the five-year average. Sunflower yields, however, are expected to remain below average, largely due to the drought in the south, where most sunflower cultivation takes place; this prediction is supported by the oblast-level analysis. However, the production outlook remains around average, as the sown area increased.

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025 | period: 2025-09 | section: Weather Review
text:
Distinctly drier-than-usual conditions prevailed across southern and eastern Ukraine during the summer months, while excessively wet conditions characterised the western regions in July. Positive thermal anomalies were observed in June and July in most regions, followed by below-average temperatures in August, except in the southern oblasts. Warmer and drier than usual conditions are forecast until late September.

The weather synthesis map summarises the most distinct anomalies during the reporting period (1 june – 9 September) compared with the 1991–2024 long-term average (LTA). Rain deficit and surplus are absolute and relative deviations from the LTA.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025 | period: 2025-09 | section: June
text:
Slightly warmer-than-usual conditions, with average daily temperatures between 0.5 °C and 1 °C above the LTA, in the south and west, but slightly colder than usual (average daily temperatures up to 1 °C below the LTA) in central northern regions and north-eastern regions; near-average conditions elsewhere.

Wetter-than-usual conditions in the northernmost oblasts, with cumulative rainfall mostly between 50% and 100% (locally up to 150%) above the LTA in northern Chernihivs’ka and Sums’ka. Drier than usual, with cumulative rainfall between 50% and 100% below the LTA, in most of the rest of Ukraine.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025 | period: 2025-09 | section: July
text:
Warmer-than-usual conditions in most of the country, with average daily temperatures between 0.5 °C and 2 °C above the LTA, especially in the east and south-east.

Significantly wetter-than-usual conditions in the west, with total rainfall up to 150%, locally more, above the LTA in northern L’vivs’ka and southern Volyns’ka, and also in most of Khmel’nyts’ka, Zhytomyrs’ka and neighbouring oblasts. Less distinct rainfall surpluses in parts of north-eastern oblasts (eastern Poltavs’ka, south-western Kharkivs’ka), with total rainfall between 50% and 100% above the LTA. Contrasting drier-than-usual conditions in most eastern and south-eastern regions, with total rainfall between 50% and 100% below the LTA.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025 | period: 2025-09 | section: August
text:
Slightly colder than usual in most northern and central oblasts, with average daily temperatures between 0.5 °C and 1 °C below the LTA, and near-average temperature conditions in southern and easternmost parts.

Drier-than-usual conditions prevailed in most of Ukraine, with total rainfall between 50% and 100% below the LTA in the regions of Volyns’ka and Rivnens’ka in the northwest, and also in Vinnyts’ka and neighbouring oblasts, in most of Odes’ka and in some eastern and south-eastern oblasts (Dnipropetrovs’ka, Zaporiz’ka, Khersons’ka, Krym). Average rainfall in the north and northeast.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025 | period: 2025-09 | section: September
text:
Observed weather, 1–9 September

Warmer-than-usual start to autumn throughout the country, with average daily temperatures between 0.5 °C and 2 °C above the LTA in most eastern regions and central northern regions, and more distinct anomalies westwards, with temperatures reaching up to 6 °C above the LTA in the westernmost oblasts.

Dry conditions, with total rainfall between 50% and 100% below the LTA, prevailed in most oblasts, except in Krym, Khersons’ka and neighbouring areas; isolated downpours in Kyyivs’ka, Khmel’nyts’ka and Zakarpats’ka.

Weather forecast, 10–19 September

Warmer-than-usual conditions are forecast for most of Ukraine, with average daily temperatures between 0.5 °C and 2 °C above the LTA in most of the eastern and some of the southern oblasts, between 2 °C and 3 °C in the western oblasts and parts of the northern oblasts and locally up to 4 °C in Vinnyts’ka and neighbouring areas. Nearaverage to slightly below-average temperatures are forecast for Krym and southern Khersons’ka.

Drier-than-usual conditions, with rainfall deficits up to 100% of the LTA, are forecast for large parts of Ukraine. In contrast, from Khmel’nits’ka westward, and in parts of Krym, cumulative rainfall is expected to exceed the LTA by up to 100% or more. The most distinct positive anomalies are forecast for Volyns’ka, Ivano-Frankivs’ka, Zakarpats’ka and eastern Krym.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025 | period: 2025-09 | section: Winter and spring crops
text:
Favourable temperatures and the absence of considerable thermal stress during the grain-filling and ripening periods maintained a positive yield outlook for winter and spring cereals in western and northern Ukraine. However, significantly drier-than-usual conditions in June negatively affected the yield formation of winter crops in the central oblasts and reinforced our below-average yield expectations in southern and south-eastern Ukraine. The harvest campaign, currently nearing completion, started on time but was delayed by abundant and frequent rainfall in July, particularly in western parts of the country, and this also led to reduced crop quality. Our updated yield forecasts confirm a fair outlook for cereals but point to below-average rapeseed yields at the national level. Recent area estimates have confirmed an increase in the area under winter crops compared with the previous campaign, supporting the overall winter crop production of the country.

Daily maximum temperatures exceeded 30 °C only for a few days in June. The absence of severe thermal stress generally supported a fair completion of the winter and spring cereals season, especially in the western and northern oblasts, where adequate soil moisture allowed crops to remain in good condition. Crop model simulations and crop-specific Sentinel-2 data (see Appendix B) confirm above-average biomass accumulation in these regions, maintaining the positive yield outlook reported in the June edition of this bulletin (1).
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025 | period: 2025-09 | section: Winter and spring crops
text:
By contrast, the rainfall deficit in some southern oblasts (Odes’ka, Mykolayivs’ka) and most central oblasts (Cherkas’ka, Kirovohrads’ka, Poltavs’ka) depleted the soil moisture content and negatively affected the grain filling of cereals, resulting in reduced yield expectations. Rapeseed, which had already suffered from a late cold spell in spring during the flowering and early pod-filling stages, was similarly impacted, resulting in a further deterioration in its yield potential at the national level. The harvest campaign for winter crops started on time at the end of June and progressed smoothly through early July before being delayed for several weeks due the abundant and frequent rainfall from mid July onward, especially in the central and western oblasts (L’vivs’ka, Volyns’ka, Khmel’nits’ka, Zhytomirs’ka). The wet conditions not only hampered fieldwork but also reduced grain quality. According to the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food (MAPF2), the harvest is nearly complete. Our updated remote-sensing-based area analysis (see Appendix A) confirms the higher rapeseed acreage reported in June, particularly in the southern oblasts (Odes’ka, Mykolayivs’ka), and points to slightly higher wheat and barley areas than our initial June estimates suggested. This finding is in line with the harvest reports at the oblast level from the Ukrainian MAPF. Our area estimates and yield forecasts at the oblast level confirm the above-average wheat and rapeseed production and the disappointing barley season at the national level.

(1) https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/jrc-news-and-updates/average-yield-outlook-winter-crops-ukrainejune-2025-2025-06-16_en.

(2) Ukrainian farmers harvested almost 30 million tons of grain crops | Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food of Ukraine.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025 | period: 2025-09 | section: Summer crops
text:
The summer crop season was marked by a cold and wet sowing campaign, resulting in delayed emergence and development throughout the season, particularly in the western oblasts. Nevertheless, the generally favourable weather conditions during summer meant that fair yield potential was maintained in this main producing area. By contrast, parts of the central oblasts, together with southern and eastern Ukraine, faced continued drier-than-usual conditions, owing to which yield prospects deteriorated. In the eastern oblasts, crop failure may even have occurred. Altogether, our remote-sensing-based area estimates and our yield forecasts point to fair national summer crop production this year, despite the disappointing sunflower yield outlook, particularly in the south.

The map displays the relative differences (in percentages) between the cumulative fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (fAPAR) from 1 August to 10 September 2025 and the medium-term average (MTA, 2015–2024) for the same period. Positive anomalies (in green) reflect above-average crop biomass, while negative anomalies (in red) reflect below-average biomass or late crop development. fAPAR data are derived from the moderateresolution imaging spectroradiometer (MODIS) on board NASA’s Terra and Aqua satellites.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025 | period: 2025-09 | section: Summer crops
text: The summer crop sowing campaign was hampered by a cold spell and abundant precipitation in early April and May and was completed in early June, with a delay of up to three weeks in sowing on average. The cool and wet spring led to slower crop emergence and early development, particularly in the western oblasts (Ternopil’s’ka, Khmel’nyts’ka, Zhytomyrs’ka). Rainfall in July ensured an adequate soil moisture supply, while August remained drier than usual. Given the nearseasonal temperatures throughout summer, grain maize, sunflower and soybean grown in western Ukraine remain delayed throughout the season, explaining the aboveaverage fAPAR signal currently observed, when a declining signal of ripening crops might usually be expected. In the central oblasts and in the north, the situation is more mixed. Delays in crop development were less pronounced and generally made up thanks to above-average temperatures in July. In the north (Chernihivs’ka, Sums’ka), a rainy June followed by near-seasonal weather later in the summer supported strong biomass accumulation. By contrast, the central oblasts (Kirovohrad’ska, Poltavs’ka) faced unfavourable conditions, with an insufficient soil moisture supply due to the overall drier-than-usual summer and two heatwaves in early and late July, leading locally to deteriorations in crop condition, with belowaverage biomass production. In the southern oblasts (Odes’ka, Mykolayivs’ka, etc.) and eastern oblasts (Dnipropetrovs’ka, Zaporiz’ka, etc.), summer crops were severely affected by persistent drought throughout the season, compromising crop and canopy development. Remote sensing images reveal significantly reduced biomass accumulation compared with previous years. Crop-specific Sentinel-2 data (see Appendix C) for grain maize, sunflower and soybean show the lowest fAPAR signal since 2019. In this part of Ukraine, crop failure may have occurred locally, and yields are forecast to be well below the five-year average. During their final reproductive stages, summer crops benefited from cooler-than-usual conditions in August across most of Ukraine.
title: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, September 2025 | period: 2025-09 | section: Summer crops
text:
This supported fair yield expectations in western parts, although the delayed phenology limited yield potential. In the north, the cooler weather further enhanced yield prospects. By contrast, it did not bring any relief to the central oblasts, where yields are projected to fall below average, or to the southern and eastern oblasts, where yields are expected to be far below average. Our yield outlook at the national level predicts aboveaverage yields for grain maize and soybean, largely produced in the central, northern and western regions, while below-average yields are forecast for sunflower, which is cultivated particularly in the central and southern oblasts. The generally drier- and warmer-than-usual weather in September allowed a timely start to the soybean and sunflower harvesting campaigns in the southern and eastern oblasts, as reported by the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food 3, albeit with reduced expectations. Only a few fields have been harvested so far in the west. Here, grain maize has not reached maturity yet, but, with above-average temperatures forecast, harvesting is expected to begin before mid-September.

3 Ukrainian farmers harvested almost 28.8 million tons of grain crops | Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food of Ukraine

text: We first derived the fAPAR profiles for all parcels before aggregating them using the crop type map described in Appendix A. This allowed to assess crop-specific development by comparing aggregated profiles with parcels represented on the same crop type from preceding years. The analysis was carried out both at the oblast level (as detailed in the crop growth conditions section) and on a 10 km grid (Figure 1). By leveraging high-resolution Sentinel-2 imagery, this approach provides a substantial improvement to the method normally employed in the bulletin, which relies on non-crop-specific MODIS data at lower spatial resolution.

section: Favourable yield outlook despite regional challenges
header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2026 | period: 2026-06 | section: Favourable yield outlook despite regional challenges
text:
Persistent dry weather since February has negatively affected winter crops in western Ukraine, while repeated cold spells in February and April reduced rapeseed yield potential in several central oblasts. Elsewhere, favourable conditions supported crop development, particularly in the south and east.

Consequently, soft wheat and winter barley yields are forecast to be above the 5-year average, whereas rapeseed yield estimates remain close to average but below the trend.

Following an exceptionally dry March, rainfall deficits persisted throughout spring in western oblasts, leading to increasing water stress during the reproductive stages of winter cereals. In contrast, winter crops in central, southern and eastern Ukraine benefited from favourable water supply. Rapeseed entered spring in good condition, but cold spells in February and April damaged flowering and early pod development, reducing the yield potential. Crop-specific Sentinel-2 profiles confirmed the contrasting regional crop development and the impact of spring frosts on rapeseed.

Despite favourable yield prospects, soft wheat and barley production remains close to the 5-year average due to the continued decline in cereal areas, particularly in non-government-controlled areas and regions close to the front line. In contrast, the rapeseed area has expanded substantially, resulting in production above both the 5-year average and the 2025 level.

The sowing campaign for summer crops was delayed by cold conditions, frost events and dry weather in March. Nevertheless, beneficial rainfall during April and early May, combined with warmer conditions from mid May onwards, improved growing conditions, and supported yield forecasts remaining close to trend.

- Distinctly warmer-than-usual conditions overall, particularly in the north-east and north-west, where daily average temperatures were 4–5 °C above the LTA. Milder positive temperature anomalies (between 1 °C and 4 °C above the LTA) elsewhere. March 2026 was among the warmest in our records since 1991, close to the record set by March 2025.

April

- Slightly colder-than-usual conditions overall, with daily average temperatures 1–3 °C below the LTA. In arable land across the country, minimum daily temperatures reached –5 °C, with two distinct cold events: the first one between 10 and 15 April, and a second, more pronounced cold spell between 27 and 30 April.

- Remarkably dry March overall, with total precipitation half or less of the usual. March 2026 was the driest in our records, followed by March 1991 and March 2011. Slightly wetter than usual only in eastern Chernivets’ka and neighbouring areas.

- Drier-than-usual conditions persisted in many western oblasts, and in the east from western Krym northward to Luhans’ka, with half or less of the usual precipitation. Some beneficial precipitation in Kharkivs’ka and neighbouring regions, as well as locally in the south/southeast, with up to 100% (locally more) of the usual precipitation.

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2026 | period: 2026-06 | section: 4.1 Winter crops
text:
Winter cereals

Winter cereals generally benefited from favourable weather around sowing and during the early vegetative development stages in autumn 2025. The exceptionally mild temperatures observed in November and December supported good establishment of crops and allowed them to survive the winter. Despite colder-than-usual conditions in January and February, widespread frost kill damage did not occur. Above-average precipitation during January across the country and during February in much of eastern Ukraine maintained adequate soil moisture reserves, enabling winter crops to resume growth in spring 2026 under generally fair conditions. From February onwards, precipitation deficits developed across large parts of western Ukraine, particularly in L’vivs’ka, Volyns’ka, Rivnens’ka and Ternopil’s’ka oblasts. Following the exceptionally dry March, below-average rainfall continued during April and early May, leading to progressively declining soil moisture reserves. Winter cereals in western oblasts entered heading and grain-filling stages under increased water stress, raising concerns for grain formation and limiting the yield potential. The impact has been most pronounced in the westernmost regions, especially L’vivs’ka, Volyns’ka oblasts and parts of Rivnens’ka and Ternopil’s’ka oblasts, where the rainfall deficit has been long lasting. The effect of the prolonged drought is clearly visible in the crop-specific Leaf Area Index

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2026 | period: 2026-06 | section: 4.1 Winter crops
text:
(LAI) profiles, which show below-average canopy development around flowering. Near-seasonal rainfall and below-average temperatures in May and early June prevented further deterioration of crop conditions. In central, southern and eastern Ukraine, in contrast, winter crops benefited from generally good water supply from early spring and until the end of the reporting period. Above-average precipitation during most of winter replenished soil moisture reserves, while subsequent rainfall supported crop development during reproductive stages without significant water or thermal stress, particularly in Vinnyts’ka, Odes’ka, Kharkivs’ka and Dnipropetrovs’ka oblasts and parts of Zaporiz’ka oblast. These favourable growing conditions are reflected in the crop-specific LAI profiles, which closely follow the development observed in the highyielding 2021 season. Yield prospects therefore remain positive in these areas. Overall, the outlook for winter cereals is contrasting across Ukraine. The reduced yield potential in the west due to prolonged drought stress is expected to be largely compensated for by favourable weather in the east and south. Consequently, national yield forecasts for wheat and barley remain close to the long-term trend but above the 5-year average, a consequence of the reduced yields observed in recent years.

Rapeseed

As for winter cereals, rapeseed saw a favourable crop establishment and suitable overwintering conditions. Mild temperatures during November and December supported crop development, and weather remained fair until the end of winter in most areas. However, the cold spell in early February with daily minimum temperatures below –20 °C in areas with limited or no protective snow cover, particularly in Kirovohrads’ka, Poltavs’ka, Cherkas’ka and Mykolayivs’ka oblasts, is expected to have caused local frost damage and reduced the yield potential there.

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2026 | period: 2026-06 | section: 4.1 Winter crops
text:
In addition, two pronounced cold spells in April, occurring between 10 and 15 April and again between 27 and 30 April, exposed rapeseed to frost during the sensitive reproductive stages of flowering and early pod formation. Minimum temperatures locally dropped below −5 °C across large parts of western and northern Ukraine, notably in Volyns’ka, Rivnens’ka, Zhytomyrs’ka, Chernihivs’ka and Sums’ka oblasts. Frost damage is likely to have resulted in flower and pod abortion, reducing yield potential in affected areas. The impact of these cold events is also reflected in the crop-specific profiles, which show a clear interruption in the vegetative phase and an inflection in the LAI signal during April.

Water supply was generally adequate in the main rapeseed-producing regions, except in the droughtaffected west. While prolonged dry conditions in western Ukraine may have further constrained yield formation, the principal concern for rapeseed this season remains the repeated cold spells in February and April. As a result, rapeseed yield prospects have deteriorated in parts of western, central and southern Ukraine. Nevertheless, crop conditions remain satisfactory in many other producing areas, particularly in Vinnyts’ka and Odes’ka oblasts and parts of Dnipropetrovs’ka oblast, and yield losses are expected to remain limited rather than widespread. Consequently, the national rapeseed yield is forecast to be slightly below the 5-year average, but substantially below the historical trend.

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2026 | period: 2026-06 | section: 4.2 Spring and summer crops
text:
Spring barley

The spring barley sowing campaign started on time, beginning in mid March in southern Ukraine. Initial sowing progress was generally satisfactory despite isolated interruptions caused by rainfall events towards the end of March. Field operations slowed more noticeably in early April, when below-average temperatures and frequent frost events constrained sowing progress across large parts of the country. Despite these constraints, sowing accelerated from mid April onwards but remained among the latest of the past decade. In most regions, sowing was completed in early to mid May, one to two weeks later than scheduled, and some fields were still being sown until late May. Cold and relatively dry soils in central and western oblasts were not favourable for spring barley emergence and early crop establishment. Crop conditions improved during May as temperatures increased and beneficial rainfall arrived. Nevertheless, crop development remains delayed compared with the seasonal average. Crop model simulations indicate overall slightly below-average leaf area development and biomass accumulation. In western Ukraine; soil moisture levels remain below average due to the persistent precipitation deficit since March and the uneven temporal distribution of rainfall. Although crop water supply is not yet critical, additional rainfall will be needed to maintain the yield potential during the grain-filling period. Conditions are generally more favourable in eastern Ukraine, where rainfall deficits are less pronounced and crop water availability is better. With delayed sowing and heterogeneous development so far, our yield forecast for spring barley at the national level remains slightly above average.

Grain maize, sunflower and soybeans

header: JRC MARS Bulletin - Global outlook: Crop monitoring in Ukraine, June 2026 | period: 2026-06 | section: 4.2 Spring and summer crops
text: The sowing of summer crops began sporadically in southern Ukraine in late March but made little progress until mid April because of freezing temperatures and cold topsoils. Warmer weather from mid April onwards has allowed the sowing of sunflowers to accelerate, while grain maize and soybean sowings have gained momentum since late April. Field operations reached full pace during May; however, the sowing campaigns remained significantly delayed compared with the seasonal average for all major summer crops. Good field accessibility was generally maintained until early May due to relatively dry topsoils. Subsequently, abundant rainfall, particularly during the second dekad of May, locally disrupted field operations and delayed sowing, especially in Sums’ka oblast. At the same time, the rain substantially improved conditions for crop emergence and early growth. The sowing of sunflowers and grain maize was nearly completed by the first dekad of June, whereas soybean sowing progressed more slowly and is still ongoing. According to the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food (1), the cultivated area of sunflowers and grain maize in government-controlled territories is expected to increase compared with 2025. In contrast, the soybean area is projected to decline considerably, although it is still expected to exceed 2 million hectares. The colder-than-usual conditions observed during the second half of April and early May resulted in a significant deficit in thermal time accumulation, creating suboptimal conditions for germination and early crop development. Early-sown crops experienced prolonged emergence and slower initial growth. In addition, severe frost events with minimum temperatures down to –6 °C around the turn of April and May may have caused local damage to emerged seedlings. As of early June, soil moisture conditions are generally favourable across most of Ukraine. Exceptions include parts of western Ukraine (Volyns’ka, L’vivs’ka and Ternopils’ka oblasts) and areas along the eastern border, particularly in Luhans’ka, Donets’ka, Zaporiz’ka and Dnipropetrovs’ka oblasts, where rainfall deficits remain substantial. Although crop development remains delayed, favourable soil moisture levels established during

May still allow for a positive outlook early in the summer crop season, provided that weather conditions during June and July remain favourable. In the short term, weather forecasts indicate a relatively cool and wet period, while the long-term weather forecasts point to near-normal temperatures in July and, albeit with high uncertainty, normal to slightly wetter-than usual conditions through the summer. The yield forecasts for summer crops remain aligned to the trend.
